META.subject: Chemistry
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 1.1 (10 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Chemistry
UNIT.content:
• Definition of chemistry
• Branches of chemistry
• Careers in chemistry
• Chemistry in our daily lives (agriculture, pharmaceutical industry, medicine, manufacturing industry, entertainment industry, nuclear chemistry, sports industry, food industry, energy among others)
• Drug, prescription, dosage and substance use
• Learner's rights and responsibilities to a safe and healthy learning environment
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the meaning of Chemistry as a field of science,
b) explore the role of Chemistry in day-to-day life,
c) examine the effects of drug and substance use in day-to-day life,
d) advocate for a safe and healthy learning environment.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner explores teamwork with peers by contributing to group decision making through recognising and acknowledging the value of others' ideas during discussions.
• Self-efficacy: The learner effectively communicates while presenting the findings on career opportunities related to Chemistry and how gender stereotypes influence career choices in plenary.
• Digital literacy: The learner uses digital technology effectively to search for information on various career opportunities related to Chemistry.
• Citizenship: The learner demonstrates critical and constructive dialogue while brainstorming with peers on the consumer rights to information on the drug prescription, substance use and knowledge on their side effects for awareness.
UNIT.values: • Respect: The learner shows acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each member as they discuss in groups the various branches of Chemistry.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: Learners generate questions about why substances such as salt, sand, sulphur, iron filings, antacid and paracetamol behave differently and add them to the Driving Question Board.
• Planning and carrying out investigations: Learners group substances by properties, mix solids with liquids, separate the mixtures and heat solids to gather evidence.
• Developing and using models: Learners build and revise a class model linking the kind of matter, its properties and its uses in daily life and medicine.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: Learners interpret observation tables of substance properties and drug label information.
• Constructing explanations: Learners explain why substances are used the way they are, such as why paracetamol is dosed and antacid is taken for acidity.
• Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information: Learners search print and digital media on careers in chemistry and communicate findings through posters and plenary presentations.
UNIT.pcis:
• Life skills (safety and security): Learners brainstorm their rights and responsibilities to a safe and healthy learning environment, including laboratory safety rules.
• Health Promotion Issues (drug and substance use): Learners discuss the meaning of drug, prescription, dosage and substance use and their effects in day-to-day life.
• Socio-Economic and Environmental issues (consumer protection): Learners explore labels on containers of manufactured products for marks of quality, expiry dates, nutritional information, preservatives and messages of caution.
UNIT.careers:
• Pharmacist / Pharmaceutical technologist: develops, dispenses and advises on medicines such as antacids and paracetamol (e.g. Kenyan pharmaceutical firms in Nairobi).
• Agricultural chemist / agronomist: fertilizers and soil testing for maize and tea farming in Kericho and the Rift Valley.
• Food technologist: preservation, quality and labelling of food products such as milk, flour and juices.
• Medical laboratory technologist and doctor: diagnosis and treatment of chronic diseases.
• Chemical engineer / industrial chemist: manufacturing of detergents, soda ash at Lake Magadi, and cement.
• Nuclear and energy chemist: nuclear energy and geothermal energy at Olkaria.
• Sports scientist: anti-doping testing for athletes.
• Forensic scientist: analysis of substances in drug-related investigations.
UNIT.focus: This unit introduces Chemistry as the study of matter, its properties, composition and changes, and shows how it shapes medicine, food, manufacturing and daily life in Kenya. Learners start by grouping everyday substances and observing what happens when they are mixed, separated and heated, then build toward the branches, importance and careers of chemistry, and the responsible use of drugs. Instruction follows a predict-observe-explain cycle anchored on the Driving Question Board and a cumulative class model.
UNIT.phenomenon: A tray at a school laboratory in Kisumu holds eight ordinary substances: table salt, water, sand, sulphur, iron filings, an antacid tablet and a paracetamol tablet. Learners are asked to sort them into groups with similar characteristics. They then mix solids with water: salt vanishes into the water, sand sinks and stays visible, iron filings are pulled out by a magnet, sulphur floats and refuses to wet, and the tablets fizz or crumble differently. Heating the solids gives different results: some melt, some burn with a blue flame and a sharp smell, and some change colour or char. Puzzling questions follow. Why do substances that all look like powders behave so differently? Why can some mixtures be separated easily while others cannot? How does knowing these properties help chemists make medicines for chronic diseases, food products and detergents with the properties they have? Learners must puzzle out why the antacid relieves heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain, and why taking too much of either is dangerous.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Medicines for chronic diseases: how are drugs such as those for hypertension or diabetes, taken daily by many Kenyans, developed, and why must the dosage on a prescription be followed exactly?
• Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? Compare salt from Lake Magadi and Mombasa salt pans, soda ash, sand and iron sheets used for roofing.
• Why are food products, detergents and man-made things around us the way they are? Examine labels of unga, cooking oil, bar soap and juice packets showing expiry dates, preservatives and cautions.
• Substance use: why do drugs such as alcohol, miraa and bhang affect the body and the learning environment differently from prescribed medicine?
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How are medicines for chronic diseases developed?
2. Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses?
3. Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding especially those that are man-made the way they are?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Phenomenon – Learners predict, sort and observe salt, water, sand, sulphur, iron filings, antacid and paracetamol tablets, record their puzzling questions and start the Driving Question Board.
Lesson 2: Matter – Learners mix solids with liquids, separate the mixtures and heat solids, then explain differences using properties and states of matter.
Lesson 3: Matter (continued) – Learners classify substances by composition and properties, and use evidence to draw the first version of the class model.
Lesson 4: Meaning of Chemistry as a field of science – Learners discuss with peers and define Chemistry, linking the definition to the evidence from the tray activity.
Lesson 5: Branches of science and chemistry – In groups, learners explore organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biochemistry and match each to the phenomenon, practising respect for others' opinions.
Lesson 6: Importance of Chemistry – Learners brainstorm and explore chemistry in agriculture, pharmaceutical, medicine, manufacturing, entertainment, nuclear, food, sports and energy industries in Kenya, and revise the model.
Lesson 7: Careers in chemistry – Learners search print and digital media for careers, discuss how gender stereotypes influence career choices and present findings in plenary.
Lesson 8: Consumer protection and product labels – Learners examine labels on product containers for quality marks, expiry dates, preservatives and cautions.
Lesson 9: Drugs and substance abuse – Learners discuss drug, prescription, dosage and substance use and examine their effects, then develop posters to sensitise peers and the community.
Lesson 10: Safe and healthy learning environment and final model – Learners brainstorm their rights and responsibilities, present posters, review the Driving Question Board and finalise the model answering how properties of substances shape the products and medicines we use.

LESSONS.title: The Kisumu Tray: Eight Substances, Many Puzzles
LESSONS.aresKeywords: phenomenon, predict, observe, sort, property, appearance, substance, dissolve, float, sink, magnet, antacid, paracetamol, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon. Learners observe and sort the eight substances on the Kisumu tray (A-H) by visible characteristics, record predictions about the water test, and write puzzling questions that start the class Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to describe the visible appearance of substances A-H (table salt, water, sand, sulphur powder, iron filings, antacid tablet, paracetamol tablet, sugar) and explain that substances can be grouped in different ways using the characteristics we can see. Learners will recognise that appearance alone cannot tell us how a substance will behave. KICD outcome link (sub-strand 1.1): explore the role of Chemistry in day-to-day life.
slo.skills: Science and Engineering Practices: Asking Questions (writing testable and puzzling questions about the tray); Making Predictions and Developing Models (recording a prediction with a reason before any test); Planning and Carrying Out Investigations (careful, safe observation without tasting); Analysing Data (comparing sorting groups across the class). Core competency: Communication and Collaboration - contributing to group decisions by recognising and acknowledging the value of others' ideas.
slo.attitudes: Respect: the learner shows acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each group member when different sorting ideas are shared. Curiosity about everyday substances and care for safe laboratory practice.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Questions: (1) How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? (2) Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? (3) Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding especially those that are man-made the way they are? Lesson 1 question: Substances A-H look alike in some ways, so why might they behave so differently?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson and builds on no earlier lesson. It launches the phenomenon and the Driving Question: How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely? Learners leave with their predictions, sorting groups and puzzling questions, which Lesson 2 will use as the starting point for testing mixing, separating and heating. The DQB started here will be revisited in later lessons. No explanations of why substances behave as they do are given in this lesson.
slo.safetyNotes: No tasting or smelling directly from any substance, including the tablets and sugar, because laboratory items are never food or medicine. Goggles on for everyone during the tray handling. Wash hands after handling. Handle iron filings and sulphur powder with a spatula or in the labelled container and do not blow on powders. Tablets are for observation only and must not be swallowed. The water test is a prediction only today. Any later heating is teacher-led. Return all materials to the tray; wipe spills straight away.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng walks into the Kisumu school laboratory with eight trays, one for each group. Each tray holds eight labelled substances: A table salt, B water (distilled, 50 mL in a beaker), C sand, D sulphur powder, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet and H sugar. Lake Victoria is just down the road, and learners think about the water, sand and salt they know from home. Learners first predict what will happen when each solid is placed in water, then observe and sort the eight substances by what they can see, feel (through the container or spatula) and compare. They notice that powders that look alike might behave differently. Wanjiru asks why the antacid and paracetamol tablets might work differently, and Mrs Achieng records this on the class Driving Question Board. The lesson ends with each group writing at least three puzzling questions on sticky notes and posting them on the DQB under the Driving Question. No water test, heat test or mixture separation is carried out today; those are saved for Lesson 2. Learners observe, predict, wonder and begin to see why chemistry matters in daily life.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in their groups of four (for example Group 1: Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir). Mrs Achieng shows the tray labelled A-H at the front but does not hand out materials yet. Learners individually write in their notebooks: (1) which of the solids A, C, D, E, F, G and H they think will dissolve in 50 mL of water at about 25 C, which will sink, which will float; (2) one reason for each prediction. They then share with their group and agree on one group prediction table with columns: Substance, Prediction (dissolves / sinks / floats / other), Reason. They are told that these are predictions only and that the actual test will be done in the next lesson. Learners also write one sentence on what they already know about how paracetamol and antacid tablets are used at home or in Kisumu clinics and pharmacies.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the tray and say: "This is the same kind of tray you will use today. Eight substances, eight letters. Before we touch anything, I want you to use what you already know from your kitchen, your shamba or the lakeshore." Display the question: "What will happen to each solid when I put one level spatula, about 2 g, into 50 mL of water at about 25 C?" Give 2 minutes of silent individual writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: "What is one thing you are very sure about, and one thing you are not sure about?" before taking responses. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups (not volunteers only) to share one prediction and reason. Say: "Thank you, Kipchirchir. Who can add to or challenge that idea respectfully?" Do not say whether any prediction is right or wrong. Write 3-4 predictions on the board. Circulate and look at the reasons being written, noting any that mention floating, sinking, 'melting into the water' or 'vanishing'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) - Predict step. Writing a prediction with a reason before any evidence makes learners' prior ideas visible to themselves and to the teacher. Later, when the class has evidence in Lesson 2, learners can compare it with these predictions and notice where their thinking changed. Individual writing before group talk gives every learner a voice (Respect).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) every learner has written a prediction and a reason for at least 5 of the 7 solids (A, C, D, E, F, G, H); (2) reasons are based on something real (for example 'salt goes into water when we make ugali water salty') rather than 'I just think so'; (3) the group table shows one agreed group prediction, with more than one learner's idea acknowledged. Note on a class list which learners offer no reason, and ask them a follow-up: "What have you seen at home that makes you think so?" Record common ideas on the board for use in Lesson 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Wearing goggles, each group receives its tray with substances A-H in labelled containers. Learners take turns using a spatula and hand lens to observe and record each substance in a table: Substance letter, name, state (solid or liquid), colour, texture or grain size (fine, coarse, powder, crystals, tablet), shape, anything else they notice (for example shiny, dull, grains that stick together). Learners pass the containers around so each learner observes all eight. They must not taste or smell directly. Learners then sort the eight substances into groups with similar characteristics using sorting cards labelled A-H. Each group chooses its own rule (for example 'white things', 'powders', 'tablets', 'things I use in food', 'things I do not think will dissolve') and records the groups. They then choose a second, different rule and sort again. Each group photographs or sketches both sorts on the group poster sheet. Learners notice puzzles, such as that salt, sugar and sand are all small grains yet may behave differently, and that antacid and paracetamol tablets both look white.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate to every group within the first 5 minutes. Ask: "What do you see? What do you notice that is the same? What is different?" Prompt Group 1: "Wanjiru, you picked up F and G. Tell me what looks alike and what looks different." Remind groups: "Goggles on, no tasting, no sniffing from the container. Use your eyes and the hand lens only." After 8 minutes ask groups to pause. Say: "Show me a different way to sort the same eight substances." WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after the question "Can the same substance belong in two different groups? Think about it." Cold-call 3 groups to share one sorting rule (not their first), and ask the class: "Which substances ended up together in more than one group? Why?" Do not tell learners the 'right' way to group; there is none yet. Do not explain solubility, magnetism or heat behaviour. If a learner asks "Will it dissolve?", answer: "Good question. Put it on your question sticky note." Check that safety rules are being followed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Sorting and Grouping (Patterns). Sorting by self-chosen rules helps learners see that the same set of substances can be grouped in many ways and that visible characteristics alone are not enough to predict behaviour. Making a second sort pushes learners to look for different features, preparing them to see the need for tests in Lesson 2. Gallery comparison across groups develops Communication and Collaboration.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every learner records at least 3 characteristics for each of substances A-H in the observation table; (2) each group produces two different sorting rules with the rule written next to each group; (3) learners use the correct names and letters (A table salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur powder, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar); (4) goggles are on and no tasting occurs. Ask a learner to explain their group's rule, and check whether another learner could apply it to a new substance, such as a tablet or crystals. Note groups whose rules rely only on colour and push them: "What else could you use?"

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their predictions and sorting groups and make sense of what they have observed so far, without explaining the science of why. In groups they complete a 'What I notice / What puzzles me' T-chart. Under 'What I notice', they list evidence from the tray (for example 'A, C and H are all small white or pale grains', 'D is yellow powder', 'E is grey and gritty', 'F and G are both white tablets'). Under 'What puzzles me', they write questions, including at least one about how substances that look alike could behave differently, one about mixing, and one about the tablets. Wanjiru's question is shared: 'The antacid tablet and the paracetamol tablet both look like white tablets, so why does one help heartburn and the other help pain?' The class discusses why both are dangerous in excess, and why a label and the Pharmacy and Poisons Board matter, but without giving the answer. Learners also say where in Kenya they have seen these substances used: salt and sugar in ugali and chai (from Mumias or Nzoia sugar), sand in building around Kisumu, iron in tools, sulphur used on crops, tablets from a chemist. They briefly discuss: Is it enough to look at a substance to know what it will do?
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "Look at your sorting and your predictions. Is looking enough to know what a substance will do? Turn and talk to your partner for 1 minute." WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners from different groups. Probe: "What makes you say that?" and "What evidence from the tray supports that?" Read Wanjiru's question aloud and say: "Wanjiru has noticed something puzzling. Who has a similar puzzle? Raise your hand if you have wondered about medicines or about why salt and sand are so different." Take 3 more responses. Say clearly: "Today we are not explaining. We are noticing and wondering. In the next lesson we will test." Avoid giving any explanation of properties, dissolving, or how medicines work. Redirect: "Great thinking. Write that on a sticky note for our board." Link to Kenyan life: "Many of you have taken paracetamol or seen an antacid at a chemist in Kisumu. Why do you think the box has a label with a number of tablets and a warning?" Take 2 responses, and say that labels will return later. Record on chart paper: 'Looking is a start, but we may need tests.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Noticing and Wondering (T-chart), with Think-Pair-Share. Separating observations from questions teaches learners to treat evidence and questions differently. Wanjiru's puzzle about the two tablets gives the class a shared, real-life question that can be traced from Lesson 1 to Lesson 10, linking the phenomenon to medicines, food and safety. Explaining is delayed on purpose so learners feel the need for evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) T-charts distinguish what was seen (observations) from what is wondered (questions); (2) at least 3 questions per group, with at least one linked to the tablets or to why powders behave differently; (3) learners say, in their own words, that appearance alone may not show how a substance behaves; (4) learners avoid giving explanations they have not tested. Ask 2 learners: "How is a question different from an observation?" Look for answers such as 'an observation is something I can see; a question is something I do not know yet.' Record who is ready to move to testing.

framework.learnerExperience: Mrs Achieng posts the Driving Question on a large sheet at the front of the Kisumu lab: "How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely?" Each group writes its best 3 puzzling questions on separate sticky notes, each with the group number. Learners come up one by one and post their notes on the DQB. As a class they cluster the questions into themes such as: (1) Why do powders behave differently? (2) Mixing and separating (for example 'Can salt be taken out of water?'). (3) Heating and burning (for example 'Why might sulphur burn?'). (4) Medicines, paracetamol, antacid (including Wanjiru's question). (5) Safety and labels ('Why is too much dangerous?'). Learners read the three KICD key inquiry questions and decide which themes link to them. A small 'Parking Lot' section is added for questions that do not fit.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "This board belongs to us. Every question you add is evidence of your thinking. There are no silly questions." Model one example from Wanjiru: "Why does one white tablet help heartburn and another help pain?" Ask: "How are our questions connected to the Driving Question?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 5 learners to read out and place a question on the board, ensuring all 8 groups are represented, including quieter learners such as Amina. Ask the class: "Which questions look alike? Where would we cluster them?" Invite one learner per cluster to suggest a heading. Ask: "Which of these questions can we investigate in the lab, and which need us to read or discuss?" Mark investigable ones with a star. Show the KICD key inquiry questions and ask: "Which of our questions fit here?" Tell learners that the board will be revisited every lesson and that the class model version 1 will be built in Lesson 3. Check that every learner has contributed at least one question and that the board is visible in the classroom.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB). The DQB turns individual curiosity into a shared, visible record of what the class wants to find out. Clustering questions into themes shows learners the structure of the topic and gives purpose to each later lesson. Returning to the board lets learners see their own progress from puzzled to explaining, which builds ownership and self-efficacy.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every group posts at least 3 questions, each written in full as a question; (2) at least half of the questions connect to the phenomenon (the tray A-H, tablets, mixing, heating, safety); (3) learners can justify a placement in a cluster with a reason; (4) learners listen respectfully when others explain a cluster (Respect). Ask 3 learners to point to a question from another group and say what they like about it. Record uncommon or advanced questions (for example about how chronic disease medicines are made) for later use. Take a photo of the DQB for the lesson record.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners begin an initial, personal 'Starting Ideas' sketch or concept map in their notebooks. At the centre they write 'Substances A-H on the Kisumu tray'. They draw arrows to their current ideas about why the substances might behave differently, using only words and ideas they already have (for example 'what it is made of', 'size of grains', 'colour', 'heat'). They add a second arrow set from the tablets to 'helps the body' and 'danger if too much'. They mark with a question mark anything they are unsure of. This is not yet the class model; it is a record of where their thinking starts. Learners then share their starting ideas with a partner and add one new idea or question from the partner. Each learner keeps the sketch for revising in Lesson 3 when the first class model (v1) is built, after evidence is gathered in Lesson 2.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Draw what you think is going on. It is fine to be uncertain. Use question marks." Show a simple example frame on the board with the centre 'Substances A-H' and two empty arrows. Give 4 minutes of silent drawing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before partner sharing. Circulate and ask: "What do you think makes salt different from sand? What makes you think so?" Cold-call 3 learners to share one idea from their sketch, including at least one with a question mark. Do not correct ideas. Say: "These are your starting ideas. In Lesson 2 you will gather evidence, and in Lesson 3 we will build our first class model, version 1, and compare it with this." Collect the sketches or ask learners to keep them safely in their notebooks. Before closing, ask learners to return all tray items, wipe benches and wash hands. Exit question: "Write one thing you are still wondering about the Kisumu tray."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial Modelling (Starting Ideas Sketch). Drawing ideas before any evidence creates a baseline model that learners can revise later. Showing uncertainty with question marks normalises not knowing and gives the teacher information about the ideas that learners bring from home and from the lakeshore. Comparing this sketch with later models makes learning visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each sketch has the centre 'Substances A-H', at least 2 ideas about why they differ, and at least one question mark; (2) the sketch links the tablets to both helping the body and danger in excess; (3) learners add at least one idea from a partner; (4) exit-ticket questions are specific (for example 'Why does sulphur float?'). Sort exit tickets into: ready to test, needs vocabulary support, and has advanced curiosity. Use these to plan groupings and prompts for Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did every learner, including quieter ones such as Amina, contribute a prediction, an observation and a question? (2) Which sorting rules did groups invent, and which important features (such as grain size, shine or being a tablet) did they miss? (3) Did learners try to explain results too early, and how did I respond without giving the answer? (4) Which DQB clusters were strongest, and which learner questions should I use first in Lesson 2? (5) Were safety rules (goggles, no tasting, no sniffing, tablets not swallowed) followed throughout? (6) Did I give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds each time and cold-call the planned numbers (4, 3, 4, 5 and 3)? (7) What ideas about medicines did learners bring from home and community, and how will I handle them respectfully? Record the common predictions about substances A, C, D, E, F, G and H so that learners can compare them with real results in Lesson 2.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe about substances A-H on the Kisumu tray? Record the colour, form (powder, crystals, grains, liquid, tablet) and any other visible features of A table salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur powder, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet and H sugar, and the sorting rules our group used.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn today? Write what we predicted for the water test and why, and what we realised about how looking alone may not tell us how a substance will behave. Also record the puzzling questions our group added to the Driving Question Board.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How can we begin to explain the phenomenon? In your own words, write your starting idea about why substances that look alike (for example salt, sugar and sand, or the antacid and paracetamol tablets) might behave differently, and one thing you will need to test in Lesson 2 to check your idea.

LESSONS.title: Matter: Mixing, Separating and Heating the Kisumu Tray
LESSONS.aresKeywords: matter, states of matter, solid, liquid, gas, property, physical property, chemical property, solubility, magnetism, density, melting, burning, filtration, magnetic separation, evaporation, dissolves, mixture M

slo.purpose: Learners gather evidence from the water test, the heat test and the separation of mixture M to explain that substances A-H behave differently because each has its own properties, which come from what it is made of. They use the particle idea of solids, liquids and gases to explain dissolving, separating and melting.
slo.knowledge: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Solids have particles tightly packed with a fixed shape and volume. Liquids have particles close together but able to move, so they have a definite volume and take the shape of the container. Gases have particles far apart, moving independently and filling the whole container. A property is a characteristic used to identify or use a substance. Physical properties include appearance, solubility, magnetism, melting point and density. Chemical properties include burning and reacting with acid. Salt (A) and sugar (H) dissolve and cannot be filtered out. Sand (C), iron filings (E) and sulphur (D) do not dissolve. Iron is removed by magnetic separation, sand by filtration, and salt by evaporation.
slo.skills: NGSS Science and Engineering Practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations (water test, heat test and separating mixture M with safe procedures); Analyzing and Interpreting Data (comparing masses of 9 g in and 8.4 g out); Constructing Explanations (linking each result to a property and to particles); Developing and Using Models (particle drawings of solid, liquid and gas, and of dissolving); Engaging in Argument from Evidence. Core competency link: Communication and Collaboration, by contributing to group decisions and acknowledging the value of others' ideas.
slo.attitudes: Respect: learners accept and appreciate the opinion of each group member when they disagree about what the evidence shows. Learners show care and responsibility for safety in the laboratory, and curiosity about why everyday substances behave differently.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Question 2: Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? Also begins to answer Key Inquiry Question 3: Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding the way they are?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 gave learners the sorting groups, water test predictions and puzzling questions about the Kisumu tray. This lesson supplies the first real evidence: it tests those predictions and shows that properties and states of matter explain the differences. It prepares Lesson 3, where learners will classify substances as elements, compounds or mixtures and build model v1 of the class DQB. It does not yet define chemistry (Lesson 4) or discuss the branches (Lesson 5).
slo.safetyNotes: Goggles on for everyone throughout. No tasting or smelling directly: waft only when told to, and only the teacher notes the smell of burning sulphur, which gives off choking sulphur dioxide, so heat sulphur near an open window or in a fume cupboard. Heating is teacher-led only, with test tubes held in holders and pointed away from people. Tie back long hair, and keep the Bunsen flame away from learners' sleeves. Do not touch hot test tubes. Wash hands after handling iron filings, sulphur and tablets. The tablets A-H are for testing only and must never be swallowed. Wipe up spills of water on the floor immediately.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns the Kisumu tray to each of the 8 groups. Learners revisit their Lesson 1 predictions and sorting groups, then test them: 1 level spatula (about 2 g) of each solid in 50 mL of water at about 25 C, followed by a teacher-led heat test and the separation of mixture M (3 g iron filings + 3 g sand + 3 g salt). They discover that substances that look alike behave very differently, then use properties and the particle ideas of solids, liquids and gases to explain what they saw, including why salt in water cannot be filtered out but sand can. They compare 9 g in and 8.4 g out to reason about loss in the procedure. Learners add new questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and sketch the first ideas that will feed model v1 in Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Lesson 1 notebooks with the sorting groups and water test predictions for substances A-H (A table salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur powder, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar). Each learner privately writes a prediction for two new tests: (1) what happens to each solid in 50 mL of water, and (2) what happens when a small amount is heated in a dry test tube. They also predict whether mixture M (iron filings, sand and salt in water) can be separated and how many grams they expect to recover from 9 g. Then in Group 1 style fours (Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir are the model group), they compare predictions and record one agreement and one disagreement on a chart, giving a reason using 'because the substance is...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your notebooks to your Lesson 1 sorting groups. Mrs Achieng's tray from Kisumu is back on your bench. Before we touch anything, I want your own prediction, in writing.' Ask: 'Which of the eight will disappear in water? Which will still be visible? Which will melt when heated? Write a reason, not just an answer.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before any talking. Circulate and cold-call 4 learners from different groups: 'Kipchirchir, what did you predict for E, the iron filings, and why?' Do not say whether predictions are right. Say: 'Wrong predictions are welcome, because they show us what to investigate.' Remind learners that no tasting is allowed. Point to a group that disagrees and say: 'Respect each other's ideas; we will let the evidence decide.' Record 3 contested predictions on the board, for example 'sulphur dissolves' and 'sugar melts like ice'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (commit-before-evidence): writing a prediction and a reason before testing makes learners' existing ideas visible and gives them something to confront with evidence. It builds understanding because learners must revise a specific claim they own, not simply receive an answer. It also links to Lesson 1 learning by reusing the sorting groups as a starting hypothesis about which substances behave alike.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) each learner has a written prediction for both tests with a reason; (2) at least 6 of 8 groups record one disagreement; (3) learners use words such as 'dissolve', 'melt', 'float' or 'sink' for at least 5 of the 8 substances; (4) the 4 cold-called learners can give a reason beyond 'I think so'. Note common ideas to address later: 'powders that look the same behave the same' and 'if it vanishes in water it has been destroyed'. Quick check: ask for a thumbs-up, sideways or down on 'I am sure about my prediction for the tablets' and note the groups showing thumbs down.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A, water test (group work, about 20 minutes): for each solid A, C, D, E, F, G and H, learners add 1 level spatula (about 2 g) to 50 mL of water (B, distilled) at about 25 C in a beaker, stir gently and record what they see. Expected observations: A salt dissolves completely to a clear colourless solution; C sand sinks, stays visible, water stays clear; D sulphur floats on top, is not wetted and stays yellow; E iron filings sink and are pulled out by a magnet, not dissolved; F antacid tablet (used whole) crumbles into a cloudy white suspension and fizzes when dropped into dilute vinegar or lemon juice; G paracetamol tablet stays mostly intact, crumbles slowly, little dissolves, and does not fizz in vinegar; H sugar dissolves completely to a clear solution. Part B, mixture M separation: learners use a magnet to remove iron (recovered 2.9 g), filter the rest to remove sand (2.8 g after drying), then evaporate the filtrate to recover salt (2.7 g). They record the masses in a table, add them to get 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g and calculate the loss: 9 - 8.4 = 0.6 g. They also try to filter a salt solution and find the salt passes through. Part C, heat test (teacher demonstration, learners observe from a safe distance with goggles on): a small amount of each solid in a dry test tube over a Bunsen flame. A salt crackles, no melting, no colour change; C sand no change; D sulphur melts to a runny yellow-brown liquid at about 115 C then burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell (sulphur dioxide); E iron filings glow orange-red and turn dull blackish; F antacid stays white and crumbles, no melting; G paracetamol melts at about 169 C and browns; H sugar melts at about 186 C, turns brown, then chars black with a caramel smell.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting say: 'Goggles on. Nobody tastes or smells anything directly. I do all the heating.' Model one test step by step for substance A, then say: 'Now you do C. Describe only what you can see, no explaining yet.' Move between the 8 groups and ask each one: 'What exactly did you see for D, the sulphur? Where is it in the beaker?' After the water test, give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds and cold-call 3 groups for results on sand, salt and iron. Ask: 'Salt vanished and sand did not. Is the salt gone?' Prompt a quick check: have a learner filter salt solution and ask 'What came through the filter paper?' For the heat demonstration, stand at the front with the window open for sulphur and say: 'Watch the colour, the flame and whether it melts. Notice the smell only if I tell you; sulphur dioxide is choking.' Cold-call 3 more learners: 'Wanjiru, what happened to H, the sugar, as it got hotter?' Ensure each group has one data table of A-H, with columns for water test, magnet, heating and mass. Check the sums: 'Add 2.9, 2.8 and 2.7. What do you get? How much did we start with? Where could 0.6 g have gone?' Accept spillage and sticking to equipment as reasons, and do not accept 'destroyed'. Use Kenyan hooks: 'Think of how salt vanishes in your ugali pot and sugar in your chai.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation table (data collection before explanation): learners fill a table of A-H with the same columns, forcing them to compare substances on the same tests. The table makes patterns visible, such as 'dissolves / does not dissolve' and 'melts / does not melt', before any explanation, which prevents learners from explaining things they did not see. The mass table for mixture M builds quantitative reasoning: learners compare 9 g in with 8.4 g out and see that separation is real but not perfect.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every group's table has entries for all 8 substances, including D burning with a blue flame and E glowing orange-red then dull blackish; (2) learners use 'dissolves' for A and H and 'does not dissolve' for C, D and E, not 'melts' or 'disappears'; (3) mass tables show 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g and a loss of 0.6 g; (4) learners can say that filtering salt solution does not remove salt; (5) safe behaviour: goggles on, no tasting, test tubes pointed away. Use a checklist and note the groups that need a re-run, such as those that did not evaporate the filtrate to dryness. If a group records 'sulphur dissolved', send them back to look at where the sulphur is in the beaker.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners explain their evidence in three steps. First, in groups, they group A-H again using properties from the evidence (for example 'dissolves in water': A and H; 'attracted by a magnet': E; 'melts on heating': D, G and H; 'burns': D; 'fizzes with acid': F) and compare this with their Lesson 1 sorting groups, noting what changed. Second, they draw a particle picture of a solid (particles tightly packed with a fixed shape and volume), a liquid (particles close but moving around, definite volume, takes the shape of its container) and a gas (particles far apart, moving independently, fill the container), and use it to explain melting of sulphur, paracetamol and sugar from solid to liquid, and the smell of sulphur dioxide spreading as a gas. Third, they write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) paragraph answering: 'Why can salt and sugar not be filtered out, but sand and iron can?' with evidence from the water test and mixture M, and they distinguish physical properties (solubility, magnetism, melting point, density) from chemical properties (burning, reacting with acid). They then use the properties to answer Wanjiru's puzzle in part: 'Why does the antacid (F) fizz in vinegar but paracetamol (G) does not?' by noting that F reacts with acid while G shows no reaction, so they are different substances with different properties.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put your Lesson 1 sorting next to your evidence table. Which groups still make sense and which need to change? Talk in your group for 3 minutes.' Ask: 'What does the evidence tell us about why substances that look like powders behave so differently?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners from 4 different groups. Press for evidence: 'Which result tells you that? Point to it in your table.' Model a particle diagram on the board for ice-like melting, using sulphur at about 115 C: 'Particles in the solid are tightly packed; with heat they move more and the solid becomes a liquid.' Ask: 'When salt dissolves, where do the salt particles go? Why can the filter paper not catch them?' (Particles are mixed in among the water particles and are too small to be caught.) Ask 2 learners to contrast filtration, magnetic separation and evaporation by using only these three terms. Give the CER sentence frame: 'My claim is... The evidence is... This happens because...' Correct: 'A substance that dissolves has not been destroyed. Evaporation brought the salt back, 2.7 g of it.' Tell learners to link physical properties (solubility, magnetism, melting point) and chemical properties (burning of D, acid reaction of F). Use the Kenyan hook: 'Chemists at Magadi separate soda ash from lake water in a similar way, using evaporation.' Close with: 'Properties come from what each substance is made of. That is why we can choose, separate and make materials.' Invite an alternative view: 'Does anyone disagree? Say it respectfully, using the evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with particle modelling: learners write a claim, back it with data from their own tables, then use the particle model of solids, liquids and gases as the reasoning that links the evidence to the claim. This builds understanding because the particle model explains why different substances respond differently, rather than just listing behaviours. Comparing the new groups with the Lesson 1 sorting is a revise-your-thinking routine that shows learners how evidence changes ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) CER paragraphs that cite at least two data points (for example 'salt dissolved to a clear solution' and 'sand stayed visible and was filtered, 2.8 g'); (2) correct use of 'dissolves' versus 'does not dissolve' and of 'filtration', 'magnetic separation' and 'evaporation'; (3) particle diagrams that show solids tightly packed, liquids close but moving, gases far apart; (4) correct sorting of at least 4 properties into physical (solubility, magnetism, melting point, density) and chemical (burning, reacting with acid); (5) at least 6 of 8 groups revise their Lesson 1 sorting with an evidence-based reason. Misconception check: if a learner says 'sugar is gone when it dissolves', ask 'How could we get it back?' and note whether they suggest evaporation. Exit ticket: 'Name one property that separates D from C and one that separates F from G.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1, which holds the driving question: 'How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely?' Each group writes 2 sticky notes: one 'We now know...' note with a finding from today's evidence (for example 'Salt and sugar dissolve and cannot be filtered out; they need evaporation') and one new 'We still wonder...' question (for example 'Why does the antacid react with acid while paracetamol does not?' or 'Why is too much paracetamol dangerous even though it does not dissolve in water much?'). They place notes next to the three KICD key inquiry questions, mark Lesson 1 questions that are now partly answered with a tick, and identify questions that need later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the Driving Question Board with your group. Read the questions from Lesson 1. Which ones can we now partly answer with today's evidence?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups write. Ask: 'Which evidence, a number or an observation, supports what you are putting on the board?' Cold-call 3 groups to read their notes aloud. Sort questions together into categories: properties and separating (answered today), classifying substances (Lesson 3), medicines and safety (later lessons). Say: 'Wanjiru's puzzle about the antacid and paracetamol is still partly open. What more would we need to know?' Do not answer fully; say: 'We will return to it.' Tell learners that the DQB will be used to build model v1 in Lesson 3. Praise respectful listening: 'I saw groups acknowledging ideas from each member. That is respect in action.' Use Kenyan context if useful: 'Which of these questions would a pharmacist in Nairobi or a chemist at a Kericho tea factory ask?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with 'We know / We wonder' notes: tracking questions publicly shows learners how evidence grows into understanding and keeps the investigation anchored to the Kisumu tray and the driving question. Sorting the notes into categories shows which questions today's evidence answered and which need new evidence, so the next lessons feel purposeful rather than random.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) each group posts one evidence-based 'We know' note and one new 'We wonder' question; (2) at least 5 groups link a note to a specific result (for example '2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g' or 'sulphur burns with a blue flame'); (3) at least 3 new questions concern medicines or safety, showing movement toward the driving question; (4) learners tick at least 3 Lesson 1 questions as partly answered; (5) learners listen to each other and acknowledge ideas without interrupting. If notes only restate observations without questions, prompt: 'What does this make you wonder about medicines, food or detergents?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners begin a draft of the cumulative class model for the Kisumu tray. On a half sheet in their notebooks, each learner sketches a two-part draft: (1) a table linking each substance (A-H) to at least one property that explains its behaviour in water or on heating, and (2) a small particle picture explaining why salt dissolves and cannot be filtered while sand does not dissolve and can be filtered. Groups then share, merge the best ideas into one group sketch, and add a 'still unsure' box (for example, 'why the antacid fizzes with acid' or 'why paracetamol melts at about 169 C yet crumbles slowly in water'). The group sketches are kept in a folder to be used in Lesson 3 to create model v1 after classification into elements, compounds and mixtures.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Today we start a draft only. This is not the final model. In Lesson 3 we will build the first full class model, version 1, after we classify the substances.' Ask: 'What must your draft explain? Think about the tray, the water test, the heat test and mixture M.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before sketching. Circulate and ask each group: 'Which property explains why E can be pulled out and C cannot?' Cold-call 3 learners: 'Amina, how does your drawing show why salt could not be filtered?' Ask for one gap in each group's draft and write it in the 'still unsure' box. Remind learners that the draft must include the phrases 'physical property' and 'chemical property' at least once. Collect folders. Close with one exit prompt: 'Complete: Today I learned that substances behave differently because ...' Preview Lesson 3: 'We will classify A-H as elements, compounds or mixtures and use your drafts to build model v1.' Tell learners to bring one example of a food or product from home with its label for later lessons, if available.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Draft modelling with gaps made explicit: learners represent their current understanding in a table and a particle sketch and note what is still unexplained. Writing a 'still unsure' box makes uncertainty a normal part of science and sets up productive revision in model v1 (Lesson 3), v2 (Lesson 6) and the final model (Lesson 10). Combining a table and a particle picture links what they observe (macro) to the particle explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each learner's table links all 8 substances to at least one property, for example A to dissolves, E to magnetism, D to burning, F to reacts with acid, G to melts at about 169 C, H to melts at about 186 C and chars; (2) particle sketches show salt particles mixed with water particles and sand particles remaining separate; (3) each group's 'still unsure' box names a specific gap; (4) exit prompts use the word 'properties'; (5) learners do not claim to have defined elements, compounds or mixtures yet, since that belongs to Lesson 3. Use a 3-point rubric: 3 = all substances linked with correct properties and a particle picture; 2 = most linked; 1 = observations only.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on: (1) Did learners move from 'they look the same' to 'each has its own properties'? Which evidence (the water test, the heat test or the mixture M masses) persuaded them most? (2) Did every learner contribute respectfully in group discussion, including quieter learners? (3) Did the safety rules (goggles, no tasting, teacher-led heating, ventilation for sulphur) hold throughout? (4) Which misconceptions persisted, such as 'dissolved means destroyed' or 'sulphur dissolves', and how will you address them in Lesson 3? (5) Which Lesson 1 questions are still unanswered, and are they on the DQB? (6) Did learners understand why 0.6 g was lost (9 - 8.4 g) without saying it was destroyed? (7) Where could local examples, such as Magadi soda ash or sugar from Mumias and Nzoia, make the ideas stronger next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Record what you observed for each of A-H in the water test and heat test, and the masses recovered from mixture M: iron 2.9 g, sand 2.8 g, salt 2.7 g, total 8.4 g, with a loss of 0.6 g from 9 g.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Write what you learned about properties of matter and states of matter: physical properties (solubility, magnetism, melting point, density) and chemical properties (burning, reacting with acid), and how solids, liquids and gases differ in their particles.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Explain in one or two sentences, using evidence, why substances that look like powders behave differently and why salt and sugar cannot be filtered out while sand and iron can be separated by filtration or magnetic separation, and how this links to the driving question about medicines, foods and safety.

reading.title: Solid, Liquid and Gas: Phases of Matter (PLIX)

LESSONS.title: Matter Continued: Classifying Substances and Building Class Model v1
LESSONS.aresKeywords: element, compound, mixture, classification, properties, separation, evidence, model v1, evaporation, filtration, magnetic separation

slo.purpose: Learners use the Lesson 2 evidence on properties and separations to classify the eight Kisumu tray substances (A-H) as elements, compounds or mixtures, and use that evidence to draw the first version (v1) of the class Driving Question Board (DQB) model.
slo.knowledge: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Element (iron E, sulphur D), compound (salt A, water B, sugar H, calcium carbonate in antacid F) and mixture (sand-iron-salt mixture M; tablets are mixtures of an active ingredient with binders). Sand C is treated as mainly silicon dioxide. Properties come from what a substance is made of. Mixtures can be separated by magnetic separation, filtration and evaporation. Recovered masses from mixture M: iron 2.9 g, sand 2.8 g, salt 2.7 g; total 8.4 g from 9 g, loss 0.6 g.
slo.skills: Classifying using evidence, analysing and interpreting data (mass recovery calculation), developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2), constructing explanations from evidence (NGSS SEP 6), communicating and collaborating in groups.
slo.attitudes: Respect: shows acceptance and appreciates the opinion of each group member while debating classifications. Curiosity and honesty in reporting evidence, including measurement loss. Safety-consciousness in handling substances (no tasting, goggles on).
slo.keyInquiry: Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? Why are food products, detergents and the man-made things around us the way they are?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave learners the WATER TEST, HEAT TEST and MIXTURE SEPARATION evidence on properties and separations. Lesson 3 asks: what are these substances made of, and can we group them by composition? It produces class model v1, which Lesson 4 uses when defining chemistry, Lesson 6 revises to v2, and Lesson 10 finalises. It moves the driving question forward by showing that a substance's properties come from what it is made of.
slo.safetyNotes: Goggles on for all hands-on work. No tasting or smelling directly any of the substances A-H (including sugar H and the tablets). Wash hands after handling iron filings, sulphur and tablets. Any heating demonstration is teacher-led only. Keep the tablets F and G away from the mouth; they are NOT sweets. Do not give children adult doses of any medicine. Wipe up spills of water immediately to prevent slipping.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns the eight Kisumu trays (A salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar) to the eight groups. Learners predict how to group the substances by what they are made of, then examine their Lesson 2 evidence: the water test, the heat test and the mixture M separation (iron 2.9 g, sand 2.8 g, salt 2.7 g, total 8.4 g, loss 0.6 g). Using a classification card sort and evidence, learners decide which are elements (D, E), compounds (A, B, H, and calcium carbonate in F), and mixtures (M, and tablets F and G as an active ingredient with binders; sand C is treated as mainly silicon dioxide). They explain why salt dissolved in water needs evaporation, not a magnet or filtration. Finally learners draw model v1 on the class DQB, linking composition to properties to uses (medicines, foods, detergents) and safety, and add new questions for later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Group 1 (Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir) and the other 7 groups receive the tray of A-H. Each learner silently writes a prediction in their notebook: 'Which of A-H do you think are made of just one kind of material, and which are made of several things mixed together? Give one reason from what we saw in Lesson 2.' Then learners place sticky notes of their predicted 'pure single substance' vs 'mixed' on a two-column chart. They connect it to the phenomenon: the antacid F and paracetamol G both look like white tablets, but do they contain just one thing?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Welcome back to the Kisumu tray. In Lesson 2 you found that A to H behave differently when mixed with water and heated. Today we ask: what are they made of?' Hold up tablet F and say: 'Is this tablet one thing or many things? Write your prediction silently.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then another 10 seconds for writing. Circulate and read at least 6 predictions. Cold-call 3 learners (one from each of three different groups): 'Which substance did you place under "mixed", and what evidence from Lesson 2 made you choose it?' Do NOT confirm or correct; say: 'Thank you, we will test these ideas with evidence.' Remind: goggles on, no tasting any substance.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas (Predict-Observe-Explain): learners commit to a prediction before seeing new evidence, which surfaces ideas such as 'powder means pure' that can be tested and revised later. Writing before talking gives every learner a voice and builds ownership of the later revision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every learner has a written prediction and a reason with a Lesson 2 observation (e.g., 'iron was pulled out by a magnet, so it is separate'); (2) teacher tallies how many sticky notes place the antacid F and paracetamol G under 'pure' vs 'mixed'; (3) the 3 cold-called learners refer to evidence, not just opinion. Note misconceptions such as 'white powder = one substance' or 'dissolved means gone'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners review their own Lesson 2 evidence and run a short, safe hands-on check. Task 1: using the recorded WATER TEST and HEAT TEST results for A-H, groups complete a data table: dissolves or not, magnet response, burns or melts. Task 2: using mixture M (3 g iron filings + 3 g sand + 3 g salt, total 9 g), groups re-trace the separation steps: magnetic separation removes iron (recovered 2.9 g), filtration removes sand (2.8 g after drying), evaporation of the filtrate recovers salt (2.7 g). Learners calculate 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g and the loss 9 - 8.4 = 0.6 g and note it is from spillage and sticking to equipment. Task 3: learners note that salt dissolved in water passes through the filter paper and cannot be removed by a magnet, so it needs evaporation. They observe that each part of M kept its own properties (iron stayed magnetic, sand stayed gritty and undissolved, salt still tasted... NOT tested, but dissolves) so M is a mixture. Learners also note the key contrast: sulphur D burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell (sulphur dioxide) while sand C shows no change on heating; sugar H melts at about 186 C, browns and chars with a caramel smell, while salt A just crackles.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Lesson 2 data. Today you are chemists checking the evidence. Which substances stayed the same in water? Which changed?' Distribute the data table and wipe-board marker. Prompt: 'Look at mixture M. After separating it, did iron, sand and salt each keep its own properties? Show me the evidence in your table.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 learners across different groups: 'Why could we not use filtration to get salt out of the water?' and 'Where did the missing 0.6 g go?' Walk to Group 1 and ask Amina: 'What does the 8.4 g tell you about how careful the group was?' Reinforce safety: 'Goggles stay on; the heat results are from the teacher-led demonstration, so no one heats anything today. Do not taste or sniff any substance.' If a group is stuck, ask: 'Which separation method uses a physical property such as magnetism, size of particle, or dissolving?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data analysis and pattern finding (NGSS SEP 4: Analysing and interpreting data): learners tabulate properties and calculate recovered mass to look for patterns, such as 'substances in a mixture keep their own properties and can be separated by physical means'. Using numbers (8.4 g, loss 0.6 g) trains evidence-based, honest reporting.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) data table complete for all 8 substances A-H with correct entries (e.g., E pulled by magnet, A and H dissolve, D burns blue); (2) correct arithmetic 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g and loss 0.6 g; (3) learners state that salt cannot be filtered out because it dissolves and needs evaporation; (4) learners use the exact terms 'filtration', 'magnetic separation' and 'evaporation'. Check with a thumbs signal and note groups needing support.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups use a classification card sort. Cards show A salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar and mixture M. Groups place each under Element, Compound or Mixture using the class definitions: element (iron E, sulphur D), compound (salt A, water B, sugar H, and calcium carbonate in F), mixture (M; tablets F and G are mixtures of an active ingredient with binders). Sand C is treated as mainly silicon dioxide. Learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) statement for two substances, for example: 'Claim: E iron filings is an element. Evidence: ... Reasoning: ...'. Learners answer Wanjiru's puzzle: 'Why does the antacid relieve heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain?' They explain that each tablet has its own active ingredient with its own properties, so the antacid reacts with and neutralises acid (it fizzes in dilute vinegar or lemon juice, while G shows no fizz), whereas paracetamol works on pain and fever by a different action. They also state that both are harmful in excess: adult paracetamol label 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets (8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g) in 24 hours; more can damage the liver; antacid taken too often can cause constipation or diarrhoea.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Chemists classify substances so they can predict how they behave. An element is one kind of substance that cannot be split into simpler ones by ordinary methods, like iron and sulphur. A compound has different elements joined together, like salt, water and sugar. A mixture has substances just mixed, each keeping its own properties.' Then: 'Use the cards and decide, with evidence.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before groups begin. Rotate between groups and ask: 'Respect each member's idea; Kipchirchir, what do you think and what does the group say?' Cold-call 4 groups to defend one classification. Ask: 'Why is the antacid tablet F a mixture even though it contains a compound, calcium carbonate?' Then ask: 'Wanjiru asked why the antacid and paracetamol differ. Using the fizz-in-vinegar evidence, who can explain?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then take 3 responses. State the safety link: 'Never give children adult doses; always follow the label or a health worker's advice; check the Pharmacy and Poisons Board approved medicines.' Do not reteach the definition of chemistry or the branches; those come in Lessons 4 and 5.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with card sort (NGSS SEP 6: Constructing explanations): learners must justify each classification with evidence from their own A-H results, linking composition to properties. Structured peer debate with equal voice practises the value of respect and exposes where ideas differ.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) card sort correct: D and E elements; A, B, H compounds; M, F and G mixtures; C treated as mainly silicon dioxide; (2) each CER statement cites at least one specific observation (e.g., 'F fizzes in vinegar, G does not'); (3) learners explain that the antacid neutralises acid while paracetamol relieves pain and fever and does not neutralise acid; (4) learners quote 4 g per 24 hours and the liver risk. Use a 3-2-1 check: three classifications justified, two properties linked, one safety rule. Record learners who respect others' views during the debate.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups return to the class DQB, which began in Lesson 1. They sort existing question cards into categories: 'What are things made of?', 'How can we separate them?', 'How do medicines work and stay safe?'. They mark questions they can now partly answer (for example, 'Why can some mixtures be separated easily while others cannot?') and write the answer with evidence on a green card beside it. They add at least one new question per group, for example 'How do chemists make a medicine for chronic diseases from these materials?', 'Why does the sugar from Mumias or Nzoia dissolve but sand does not?' and 'Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses?'. Group 1 links the 0.6 g loss to a question about how factories in Kenya, such as Magadi soda ash, avoid wasting material.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question: how do the different properties of substances help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely? Which question cards can we now answer, even partly?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Invite 3 learners to place a green evidence card and read it aloud. Cold-call 2 groups to share their new question and say which KICD key inquiry question it links to. Ask: 'Which questions are still open? Where will we look for the answers?' Star at least 2 open questions for Lessons 4 to 9 (for example, the meaning of chemistry, branches, industries, labels and drug use). Praise respectful listening: 'Thank you for acknowledging each other's ideas.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: separating answered, partly answered and open questions makes progress visible and keeps learners' curiosity steering the unit. Connecting each card to evidence reinforces that scientific claims need data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each group posts at least one evidence-backed answer card and one new question; (2) at least 2 new questions connect composition or properties to medicines, foods or detergents; (3) learners can name a KICD key inquiry question that matches their card; (4) teacher notes which questions show persistent misconceptions (for example, 'dissolved salt disappears').

framework.learnerExperience: Each group draws model v1 on a chart paper for the class DQB model. The model shows: Matter (anything with mass that occupies space) at the top; three boxes: element (D sulphur, E iron), compound (A salt, B water, H sugar, calcium carbonate in F) and mixture (M, F, G); arrows from composition to properties (solubility, magnetism, burning, melting, reaction with acid) and then to uses and separations: magnetic separation, filtration and evaporation. A section labelled 'Medicines and safety' shows the antacid neutralises acid, paracetamol relieves pain and fever, and the 4 g per 24 hours maximum with the liver warning. Groups add a 'We are not sure yet' box. Groups present in a gallery walk and one representative from each group explains one arrow using evidence. The class agrees on one shared v1 and keeps it for revision in Lesson 6 (v2) and Lesson 10 (final).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is a tool for explaining and predicting. Draw what you think explains why A to H behave differently and how that helps chemists make medicines, foods and detergents safely.' Show the required parts: matter, three classes, properties, uses and safety. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before groups start drawing. Circulate and ask: 'Which piece of evidence supports this arrow? What would you change if mixture M had lost 2 g instead of 0.6 g?' Hold a gallery walk of 5 minutes; learners leave one sticky note with a 'star' (what is strong) and one 'wish' (what is missing). Cold-call 3 groups to explain one arrow. Then combine into one class v1 on the DQB wall and say: 'This is version 1; it is allowed to be incomplete. We will revise it in Lesson 6 and finalise it in Lesson 10.' Close with an exit ticket: 'Write one sentence explaining why iron and sulphur are elements while salt is a compound, using evidence.' Remind learners to wash their hands and leave the trays tidy.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): learners represent relationships among composition, properties, separations and safe use in one diagram. Peer gallery walk with star and wish feedback develops critique skills, and labelling uncertainty teaches that models are revised as new evidence arrives.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) model v1 includes matter, the three classes with correct examples, properties, separation methods and the medicine-safety link; (2) at least two arrows are supported with a specific piece of evidence; (3) a 'not sure yet' box is present; (4) the exit ticket correctly says that iron and sulphur are each a single kind of substance (elements), while salt is a compound. Collect exit tickets and sort into secure, partly secure and needs support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believe that a white powder or a tablet is automatically a single substance, and what evidence changed (or did not change) their minds? Did every group member, including quieter learners such as those in Group 1, contribute to the card sort and the model with respect shown to others' ideas? Were the 0.6 g loss and the 4 g per 24 hours limit understood as real data rather than numbers to memorise? Which model v1 gaps (for example, why elements and compounds differ at a deeper level) should be noted on the DQB for later lessons, and how will Lesson 4 build on this evidence without re-teaching it?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that A salt and H sugar dissolve completely, C sand and E iron filings do not dissolve, E is pulled out by a magnet, D sulphur floats and burns with a blue flame and sharp smell, and F antacid fizzes in vinegar while G paracetamol does not. In mixture M we recovered iron 2.9 g, sand 2.8 g and salt 2.7 g, a total of 8.4 g out of 9 g, so 0.6 g was lost.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that substances can be classified as elements (D sulphur, E iron), compounds (A salt, B water, H sugar, calcium carbonate in F) or mixtures (M, and tablets F and G with binders). Mixtures can be separated by magnetic separation, filtration and evaporation, but dissolved salt needs evaporation. Class model v1 links composition to properties to uses and safety.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The substances behave differently because each has its own properties, which come from what it is made of. Iron and sand can be pulled out or filtered, while salt and sugar dissolve and cannot be filtered out. The antacid works because it neutralises acid, paracetamol works on pain and fever by a different action, and both are harmful in excess, so we follow labels and correct dosage.
