LESSONS.title: Meaning of Chemistry as a Field of Science: Defining Chemistry from the Tray Evidence
LESSONS.aresKeywords: chemistry, matter, composition, properties, changes, uses, evidence, definition, tray substances A-H, DQB

slo.purpose: Learners explain the meaning of Chemistry as a field of science by building a definition from the Kisumu tray evidence (substances A-H) and testing it against their own observations.
slo.knowledge: Chemistry is the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space, and exists as solid, liquid or gas. Each tray substance has its own properties (solubility, magnetism, melting and burning behaviour, reaction with acid) that come from what it is made of. Chemists use these properties to choose, separate and make materials such as medicines, foods and detergents.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations from evidence; communicating and collaborating in pairs and groups (KICD core competency: contributing to group decision making by recognising and acknowledging the value of others' ideas); analysing and interpreting data from the tray observations; developing and refining a definition (NGSS SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Respect: learners show acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each member as they discuss and refine the definition. Curiosity about how chemists use properties of substances to make safe products.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry questions: (1) How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? (2) Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? (3) Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding, especially those that are man-made, the way they are? This lesson answers the first part of each by asking: What is Chemistry, and what in our tray evidence shows it is the science of matter?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 3 gave learners the Kisumu tray observations, the properties and separation evidence, the classification of substances and class model v1. Lesson 4 gives learners the language to name what they have been doing: Chemistry. The class definition becomes the foundation for Lesson 5 (the five branches) and later lessons on industries, careers, labels and drugs, and it advances the driving question by showing that knowing properties is the heart of how chemists make products and keep people safe.
slo.safetyNotes: No new practical work is done. If learners handle tray substances for re-observation, goggles must be worn, nothing is tasted or put near the mouth (including the antacid F, paracetamol G and sugar H), hands are washed after handling, and heating is done only by Mrs Achieng or under her direct supervision. Paracetamol and antacid tablets are used for observation only and are never swallowed in class. Remind learners that medicines are taken only as advised on the label or by a health worker.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns the groups to their Kisumu trays (A table salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar). Learners first predict what Chemistry means and what chemists study, then gather evidence by sorting their own tray observations into the categories composition, properties, changes and uses. In the Explain phase they build a class definition, test it against specific evidence (salt and sugar dissolving, sand and iron not dissolving, sulphur burning, paracetamol melting at about 169 C, the antacid fizzing in vinegar) and apply it to the medicine puzzle raised by Wanjiru. They then add new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise the definition section of model v1 so it names Chemistry as the science that studies matter.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in their groups of four (for example Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir in Group 1) beside the tray of substances A-H. Individually, for 2 minutes, each writes in the notebook: 'I think Chemistry is the study of ______ because when we tested the tray, we ______.' They also list two things they believe a chemist in Kisumu, Mombasa or Nairobi does. Then they share with a partner and the pair agrees on one prediction sentence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we classified A to H as elements, compounds and mixtures and built model v1. Today we name the science we have been doing. Before I tell you anything, write what you think Chemistry is.' Display the DQB and the tray. After the question, give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before anyone writes. Walk around and note recurring words (substances, mixing, medicine). Cold-call 4 learners from different groups to read their pair's sentence without comment. Say: 'Thank you, I am not marking right or wrong yet. We will test these ideas against our evidence.' Record 4 predictions on the board under the heading 'Our first ideas about Chemistry'. Remind the class that all ideas are valued and respectful listening is expected.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Revisit: learners commit to an idea before instruction so their later revision is visible to themselves. Writing the sentence first, then sharing with a partner, surfaces prior ideas, including misconceptions such as 'Chemistry is only about dangerous liquids and laboratories', and creates a baseline to compare against the final definition.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether predictions mention substances, properties, medicines or changes (versus only 'experiments'). Indicators: at least 4 of 8 groups include 'substances' or 'materials' in their sentence; note learners who link to a tray result (for example 'salt vanished in water'). Tally misconceptions (Chemistry = only chemicals that are dangerous; Chemistry = only lab work) on a teacher checklist to address in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners review their own recorded observations from Lessons 1-3 (water test, heat test, mixture separation, classification) and the tray in front of them. Each group receives a four-column evidence chart headed Composition (what it is made of), Properties, Changes, Uses. Using their data, they fill in at least one row per substance for six chosen substances (A to H, minimum six). Examples: A salt dissolves completely in water and crackles but does not melt when heated; C sand sinks, stays visible and does not change when heated; D sulphur floats, melts at about 115 C then burns with a blue flame and sharp choking smell (sulphur dioxide); E iron filings are pulled out by a magnet and glow orange-red then turn dull blackish when heated; F antacid crumbles into a cloudy white suspension and fizzes in dilute vinegar; G paracetamol stays mostly intact in water, does not fizz, melts at about 169 C and browns; H sugar dissolves, melts at about 186 C, turns brown then chars black with a caramel smell. They also use mixture M: 9 g in, 8.4 g recovered (2.9 g iron, 2.8 g sand, 2.7 g salt), loss 0.6 g. Learners may briefly handle the tray substances with goggles on and no tasting to re-check a result.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are chemists today. Sort what you already know about A to H into four columns. Use only evidence from your own results.' Model one row on the board (A table salt: composition: sodium chloride, a compound; property: dissolves completely, clear colourless solution; change: crackles but no melting when heated; use: seasoning food, for example in ugali and nyama choma). Circulate to every group at least once and ask: 'Which column does the blue flame of sulphur belong in, and why?' and 'Where does the magnet separating E from the mixture M belong?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before prompting. Check safety: goggles on, no tasting, tablets not swallowed. Cold-call 3 groups to read one row aloud and ask the class to point to the evidence in their own notes. Praise respectful use of others' ideas, for example 'I like how Amina asked Kipchirchir to explain his row before adding hers.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Sorting with a Four-Column Chart (Composition, Properties, Changes, Uses): learners organise familiar data under the categories that will become the parts of the definition. This turns scattered observations into patterns (every substance has a composition and properties, many show changes, and uses follow from properties) and prepares them to build the definition from evidence rather than memorising it.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check charts for accuracy against the established results: salt and sugar listed as dissolving, sand, iron and sulphur as not dissolving; sulphur burning blue; paracetamol melting at about 169 C; sugar melting at about 186 C. Indicator: at least 6 substances entered with at least three of the four columns filled. Watch for property/change confusion (for example listing 'burns' as a property of sand) and for correct use of letters A-H. Note which groups can link a use (such as antacid for heartburn) to a property (reacts with and neutralises acid).

framework.learnerExperience: 1) Think-Pair-Share: pairs scan their chart and write answers to 'What do all four columns have in common?' (they all describe matter, anything that has mass and occupies space). 2) Groups use sentence frames to draft a definition: 'Chemistry is the science that studies ______, including its ______, ______, ______ and ______.' 3) Groups present drafts to the class; the class compares and negotiates one agreed class definition: Chemistry is the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. 4) Learners test the definition against three challenge cases: (a) Does it explain why salt dissolves but sand does not? (b) Does it explain how the mixture M was separated by a magnet, filtration and evaporation? (c) Wanjiru's question: why does the antacid F relieve heartburn while paracetamol G relieves pain? They explain that the antacid reacts with and neutralises excess stomach acid (it fizzes in vinegar) while paracetamol relieves pain and fever by a different action and does not neutralise acid. 5) Learners state why taking too much of either is dangerous: paracetamol maximum 8 tablets x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g in 24 hours, more can damage the liver; too much antacid can upset the body's salts and cause constipation or diarrhoea. Each learner finishes by writing the agreed definition in their own words and linking it to one piece of tray evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your four columns. What is the same about every substance on this tray?' Wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Introduce the term matter: 'Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Water, sand, a tablet and the air in this room are all matter.' Briefly remind learners of solids, liquids and gases without re-teaching Lessons 2 and 3. Give groups 4 minutes to draft the definition. Select 3 groups to present (different wording, for example one group that stresses uses). Write the common words on the board and negotiate: 'Which words do all three drafts share? What is still missing?' Then give the conventions definition and have learners compare it to the class version. For challenge case (c), say: 'Wanjiru asked this in Lesson 1. Use the definition to explain what you now understand.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners across groups. Stress the safety message: 'Chemistry also helps us recognise the risks of drug abuse and develop safe medicines. Always follow the label or a health worker; never give children adult doses.' Address misconceptions noted earlier (Chemistry is not only dangerous liquids; it studies all matter, including ugali, tea from Kericho and the water in Lake Victoria). Do not teach the five branches here; say: 'Next lesson we will see that Chemistry has branches.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Consensus Discourse: learners make a claim (the definition), support it with specific tray evidence, and reason why the evidence supports each part of it. Negotiating a class definition from several group drafts builds shared ownership, and testing the definition on challenge cases (including the medicine puzzle) shows that a good definition can explain real phenomena, not just be recited.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for definitions that include matter plus at least three of composition, properties, changes and uses. Indicators: learners cite specific evidence (for example 'Sulphur D melts at about 115 C then burns, which is a change, so Chemistry studies changes'); learners correctly explain that the antacid neutralises acid and paracetamol does not; learners state the 4 g maximum correctly; learners acknowledge a peer's idea respectfully during negotiation. Use a quick 3-finger check (3 = confident to explain, 1 = need help) and revisit with groups showing 1.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board. In groups, they discuss: 'Which of our earlier questions can we now answer using the definition of Chemistry?' They place sticky notes on answered questions with the evidence (for example 'Why do powders behave differently? Because each has its own composition and properties'). Each group then writes at least one new question that this lesson raises, such as 'What are the different areas of Chemistry?', 'Who works as a chemist in Kenya?', 'How do chemists in Nairobi make sure medicines are safe?' or 'Why does the label on paracetamol give a maximum number of tablets?' and adds it to the board under 'Questions to answer next'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our driving question asks how properties help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how we use them safely. Which of our questions can we now answer?' Wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to move one answered question and read the evidence. Cold-call 2 more groups for new questions and ask: 'What in today's lesson made you ask that?' Group new questions into likely lessons: branches (Lesson 5), industries (Lesson 6), careers (Lesson 7), labels (Lesson 8), drugs and substance abuse (Lesson 9). Say: 'We will return to these as we gather more evidence.' Ensure that every group contributes at least one note and that contributions are acknowledged respectfully.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a Public Record of Learning: the board makes visible what the class has figured out and what remains puzzling. Linking questions to evidence turns answered questions into claims, and new questions created from the definition show learners that understanding grows in steps and guides the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group adds at least one new question and moves at least one answered question with evidence. Indicators: new questions refer to the definition or the tray (not generic questions); answered questions cite A-H data. Note groups whose questions are only recall (for example 'What is Chemistry?') and prompt them to ask 'how' or 'why' questions linked to medicines, foods or detergents.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit class model v1 (from Lesson 3), which classified A-H as elements, compounds and mixtures. In groups they add a header or box to the model: 'Chemistry = the science that studies matter: composition, properties, changes and uses.' They draw arrows linking at least three tray examples to the parts of the definition: composition (D sulphur and E iron are elements; A salt, B water and H sugar are compounds; mixture M is a mixture), properties (salt dissolves, iron is magnetic), changes (sulphur burns, sugar chars) and uses (antacid for heartburn, paracetamol for pain and fever). Each group writes one sentence on how the definition helps explain Wanjiru's question about the antacid and paracetamol. They add an arrow labelled 'safe use: label and dosage' pointing to the medicines. A volunteer from each of 2 groups explains their addition to the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model v1 shows how we classify the substances. Now add what the whole science is about.' Display model v1 and model one addition (for example an arrow from A salt to 'properties: dissolves in water'). Circulate and ask: 'Which part of the definition does this arrow show?' and 'What evidence supports it?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 2 groups to share. Say: 'This is not the final model. In Lesson 6 we will revise it to version 2 after we study how Chemistry is used in industries such as Magadi soda ash, Kericho tea and Mumias sugar.' Close with a 1-minute exit ticket: 'Write the class definition of Chemistry and give one piece of evidence from tray substances A-H.' Collect the tickets.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners add the new idea (the definition of Chemistry) to the existing model v1 and connect it to earlier evidence. Drawing arrows between a general definition and specific data shows how big ideas are supported by evidence and prepares for later revisions (v2 in Lesson 6 and the final model in Lesson 10).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the models for at least three correct links between tray evidence and parts of the definition and for the use of letters A-H. Exit ticket indicators: includes 'matter' and at least three of composition, properties, changes, uses; gives one accurate piece of evidence (for example F fizzes in vinegar, so the antacid reacts with acid). Sort tickets into secure, partly secure and not yet secure, and plan a short revisit at the start of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners build the definition from evidence in their own words, or did they wait for the teacher's version? Which tray observations did learners use most readily as evidence, and which were harder to place in the four columns (composition vs properties vs changes)? Did any learners still think Chemistry is only about dangerous liquids or laboratory work? Were all voices heard in group discussion, and did learners show respect when negotiating the class definition? Did the medicine puzzle (antacid, paracetamol and the 4 g maximum) help learners see why Chemistry matters for safety? What adjustments are needed before Lesson 5, when learners match the five branches to parts of the phenomenon?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did you observe about the tray substances A-H that shows Chemistry studies matter? For example: salt A and sugar H dissolve, sand C and iron E do not, sulphur D burns with a blue flame, and the antacid F fizzes in vinegar while paracetamol G does not.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did you learn about the meaning of Chemistry? Chemistry is the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does the definition of Chemistry help explain why the antacid relieves heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain, and why chemists in Kenya need to know the properties of substances to make medicines, foods and detergents safely?

LESSONS.title: Branches of Chemistry: Matching the Five Branches to the Kisumu Tray
LESSONS.aresKeywords: branches of chemistry, organic chemistry, inorganic chemistry, physical chemistry, analytical chemistry, biochemistry, respect, Kisumu tray, mixture M

slo.purpose: Learners explore the five branches of chemistry (organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biochemistry) and match each to part of the Kisumu tray phenomenon, while showing respect for each member's opinion in group discussion.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to name the five branches of chemistry and say what each studies. They will match sugar (H) and paracetamol (G) to organic, salt (A) and iron filings (E) to inorganic, melting points (sulphur about 115 C, paracetamol about 169 C, sugar about 186 C) to physical, the separation of mixture M to analytical, and how the antacid (F) and paracetamol (G) act in the body to biochemistry.
slo.skills: Discussing in groups, matching evidence to categories, justifying a claim with evidence from the tray (Constructing Explanations), communicating ideas respectfully, and using the Lesson 4 definition of chemistry to reason.
slo.attitudes: Respect: the learner shows acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each member as they discuss in groups the various branches of Chemistry. Learners also develop curiosity about how chemists work in Kenya.
slo.keyInquiry: Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? (Learners start from the tray and ask which branch of chemistry would answer each puzzling question.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 4 defined chemistry as the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Lesson 5 shows that this science has five branches, each answering a different question about the tray. This gives learners a vocabulary to sort their DQB questions and prepares them for Lesson 6, where they study how chemistry is used in Kenyan industries and revise the class model to v2.
slo.safetyNotes: No tasting or smelling any substance. Goggles on if any tray substance is handled. Tablets (F and G) are looked at only and are not eaten; they must not be taken from the lab. Sulphur (D) and iron filings (E) are handled only with spatulas. No heating in this lesson. Use data from earlier lessons and the lesson cards, not new demonstrations. Respectful talk rules apply: one speaker at a time, and build on or politely challenge ideas.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns to the Kisumu tray (A salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar). Learners recall the Lesson 4 definition of chemistry and predict what 'branches' of chemistry might mean. In Group 1 (Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir) and the other seven groups, they rotate through five evidence cards, one per branch, using the tray results already collected: sugar and paracetamol, salt and iron, melting points, separation of mixture M (recovered 2.9 g, 2.8 g and 2.7 g; loss 0.6 g), and the action of the antacid and paracetamol. Groups match each card to a branch, justify the match, and practise respect through talk norms and a listening check. The class then sorts DQB questions by branch and adds the five branches to the model notes ahead of v2 in Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the tray (A-H) and the Lesson 4 definition on the board: chemistry is the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Individually they write in two minutes: 'Chemistry is one science, but chemists do different jobs. Which different questions about our tray might different chemists ask?' They then share with a partner, and groups write one prediction of what 'branches of chemistry' means and put a ? next to any word they are unsure of.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we defined chemistry. Today we ask: does every chemist study the same thing about this tray?' Point to A-H. Ask learners to write silently for 2 minutes. Then pose: 'Which question about the tray would YOU like a chemist to answer first?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Cold-call 4 learners (including at least one from the back row) and write their questions on the board without evaluating. Say: 'Thank you. I will not tell you if this is right yet. We will test it with evidence.' Remind the class of the respect norm: 'In this lesson, every opinion is heard before we decide.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior knowledge through a Predict-Write-Pair-Share routine: learners commit ideas in writing before discussion. This surfaces what they already think about chemistry and makes later revision of ideas visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 80% of learners writing a question or prediction within 2 minutes; (2) predictions that mention properties, medicines, separation or food; (3) learners using the words 'matter', 'properties' or 'substances' from Lesson 4. Note learners who write only 'I do not know' for targeted support during group work.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners rotate through five evidence cards placed at stations on the lab benches, spending about 4 minutes at each. Each card gives data already collected from the tray: Card 1: H sugar and G paracetamol (made of carbon-containing substances; sugar melts at about 186 C, turns brown, then chars black with a caramel smell; paracetamol melts at about 169 C and browns). Card 2: A salt and E iron filings (a salt dissolves completely; iron is pulled out by a magnet and glows orange-red then turns dull blackish when heated). Card 3: Melting points: D sulphur melts at about 115 C, G paracetamol at about 169 C, H sugar at about 186 C; A salt crackles without melting and C sand does not change. Card 4: Mixture M (3 g iron + 3 g sand + 3 g salt = 9 g): magnet recovers 2.9 g, filtration recovers 2.8 g, evaporation recovers 2.7 g; total 8.4 g, loss 0.6 g. Card 5: F antacid neutralises excess stomach acid and fizzes in dilute vinegar; G paracetamol relieves pain and fever, does not fizz in vinegar and does not neutralise acid; too much of either is harmful (maximum 8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours for adult paracetamol). At each station, learners record what the card shows and a first guess at which branch it belongs to. Each learner takes a role: reader, recorder, timekeeper or respect-checker (Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir rotate roles in Group 1).
framework.teacherMoves: Before rotation, display the five branch names with one-line meanings: organic (substances based on carbon, such as sugar and many medicines), inorganic (substances such as salts, metals and minerals), physical (how matter behaves, such as melting points and energy changes), analytical (finding out what is present and separating or measuring it), biochemistry (chemistry of living things, including how medicines act in the body). Say: 'Read the card, then ask your group: what is this card measuring or explaining?' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which words on the card made you think of that branch?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 2 recorders per round for one-sentence reports. Do not give the matches; if a group is stuck, say: 'Look at the verb on the card: separate, melt, act in the body, contain carbon, element or salt.' Safety: reinforce no tasting and no handling tablets beyond looking.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-based categorising (Analysing and Interpreting Data): learners sort real tray data into categories and justify each match with a specific piece of evidence. Rotating stations spreads the data across the room and gives every learner a defined role, which supports respectful sharing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) recorders write the branch name AND one data point (for example '169 C' or '2.9 g') for each card; (2) in each group every member speaks at least once at each station; (3) the respect-checker marks one example of a group member building on another's idea. Note groups that assign branches using only the substance name without data.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups return to their desks and complete a matching table: Branch | Part of the Kisumu phenomenon | Evidence | Why this branch? Each group must explain one disagreement they had and how they resolved it respectfully. Then groups face the puzzle: 'Wanjiru asked why the antacid relieves heartburn but paracetamol relieves pain. Which branches help answer that question?' Learners argue that biochemistry explains how each acts in the body, inorganic or physical chemistry helps explain why the antacid neutralises acid, and organic chemistry helps explain what paracetamol is made of. They also note that one tray substance can belong to more than one branch (for example paracetamol G is studied by organic chemistry for its makeup and by biochemistry for its action). Groups share a claim, evidence and reasoning to the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Choose the branch you think fits best, and tell us the evidence. Remember: we listen first, then we agree or politely disagree.' Model a respectful sentence frame on the board: 'I understand your idea that ___. My evidence suggests ___.' Cold-call 3 different groups to give one match and defend it. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking another group to respond. Ask: 'Can one substance belong to two branches? Which one, and why?' Ask Group 1 to explain how Wanjiru's puzzling question connects to biochemistry. Correct misconceptions: that each substance belongs to only one branch; that 'organic' only means farming without chemicals (here it means carbon-based substances). Confirm expected matches without over-teaching: sugar and paracetamol (organic), salt and iron (inorganic), melting points (physical), separation of mixture M (analytical), antacid and paracetamol action (biochemistry). Do not re-teach the classification of elements, compounds and mixtures (Lesson 3) or the definition of chemistry (Lesson 4); only refer to them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (Constructing Explanations) with a respectful discussion protocol: learners state a claim, support it with tray data, and explain the reasoning linking the data to the branch. Using sentence frames for agreeing and disagreeing makes acceptance of others' opinions an explicit part of the thinking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) at least 6 of 8 groups correctly match all five branches with at least one piece of data each; (2) learners can state that paracetamol G fits more than one branch; (3) learners use the sentence frame when responding to another group; (4) correct statement that mixture M separation (magnet 2.9 g, filtration 2.8 g, evaporation 2.7 g) is analytical chemistry. Probe any group that mixes up physical and analytical by asking: 'Is this about how matter behaves, or about finding out and separating what is in it?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the class DQB with questions from Lessons 1-4. In groups they place a sticky note with a branch label (O, I, P, A or B) next to at least two existing questions, for example 'Why do powders behave so differently?' (physical or inorganic), 'Why can some mixtures be separated easily?' (analytical), 'How do medicines work and why is too much dangerous?' (biochemistry and organic). Each group writes one new question that a chemist in a specific branch could investigate, for example 'How do chemists in Nairobi pharmaceutical companies check that every paracetamol tablet contains 500 mg?' (analytical) or 'How can we test which Magadi soda ash is pure?' (analytical or inorganic). Groups explain the label they chose to another group.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board has many questions. Today we sort them by which branch could help answer them.' Model one example on the board. Give each group 3 sticky notes. Ask: 'Which questions cannot be answered by one branch alone?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to read one new question and say which branch would investigate it. Ask the class to respond respectfully: 'Does anyone see a different branch? Tell us why.' Point out that the key inquiry questions (How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? Do all substances have the same properties and uses? Why are food products, detergents and man-made things the way they are?) need several branches. Mark questions that remain unanswered for Lesson 6, where industries and model v2 will be studied.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question sorting on the DQB (Asking Questions): linking each question to a branch shows learners how a big driving question breaks into smaller investigable questions, and keeps the board as a record of growing understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every group places at least 2 branch labels on existing questions and writes 1 new question; (2) at least half of the new questions refer to a tray substance (A-H) or mixture M; (3) learners can justify a label in one sentence using evidence. Note questions that are about careers or labels and flag them for Lessons 7 and 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their model notes (class model v1 from Lesson 3 remains the current version) and add a 'Branches' section under the heading 'How chemists study the tray'. Each learner draws or lists a simple diagram with the tray at the centre and five arrows labelled with the five branches, each with one example from the tray (organic: sugar H and paracetamol G; inorganic: salt A and iron E; physical: melting points; analytical: separation of mixture M; biochemistry: action of antacid F and paracetamol G). Learners also write a respect reflection: one idea from another member that improved their group's answer. These notes will feed the revision to model v2 in Lesson 6.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model v1 explains why substances differ. Now add: who studies which part?' Give 5 minutes for writing. Walk around and ask: 'Which branch would you need to check that two tablets contain the same amount of paracetamol?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to read their respect reflection or one diagram label. Close with: 'Which branch do you think helps most with safe use of medicines, and why? Keep your answer for next lesson.' Remind learners that the DQB will be revisited in Lesson 6 when we look at Kenyan industries and revise the model to v2. Collect model notes to check understanding.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building (Developing and Using Models): learners add a new layer (branches) to the existing model notes without discarding earlier ideas, showing that models grow as evidence increases. The respect reflection links the scientific practice of listening to peers' ideas with improving the group's model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) diagram includes all five branches with one correct tray example each; (2) at least 80% of learners write a specific respect reflection naming an idea from a peer; (3) learners can state in their own words that chemists in different branches study different aspects of the same substances. Use the collected notes to plan reteaching of physical versus analytical in the next lesson opener if needed.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did every learner contribute to the group discussion, or did a few dominate? Which branch was hardest to match (for example physical versus analytical), and what evidence helped learners decide? Did learners realise that one substance, such as paracetamol G, can belong to more than one branch? How well did the sentence frames support respectful disagreement? Which DQB questions are still unanswered and need Lesson 6 (importance of chemistry in Kenya and model v2) or later lessons on careers, labels and drugs? What would I change about the station timing or roles next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed data from the Kisumu tray: sugar H and paracetamol G melt and brown at about 186 C and 169 C; salt A dissolves and iron E is pulled out by a magnet; sulphur D melts at about 115 C; mixture M (9 g) was separated by magnet (2.9 g), filtration (2.8 g) and evaporation (2.7 g); the antacid F fizzes in vinegar while paracetamol G does not.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Chemistry has five branches: organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biochemistry. Each answers different questions about the same substances, and one substance can belong to more than one branch. Listening respectfully to every group member's opinion improved our answers.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The tray puzzles are answered by different branches working together: organic (sugar H and paracetamol G), inorganic (salt A and iron E), physical (melting points), analytical (separating mixture M) and biochemistry (how the antacid F and paracetamol G act in the body). This helps chemists make and test medicines, foods and other products safely, which moves us toward answering the driving question.
