LESSONS.title: Importance of Chemistry in Kenya: From the Kisumu Tray to Our Industries (Model v2)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: importance of chemistry, agriculture, pharmaceutical industry, medicine, manufacturing, entertainment, nuclear chemistry, food, sports, energy, model v2, Kenya industries

slo.purpose: Learners explore the role of Chemistry in day-to-day life by linking the properties of substances A-H from the Kisumu tray to how chemistry is used in Kenyan agriculture, pharmaceutical, medicine, manufacturing, entertainment, nuclear, food, sports and energy industries, and then revise the class model from v1 to v2.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (1) industries choose, separate and make materials using properties such as solubility, magnetism, melting point, burning and reaction with acid; (2) the antacid (F) works because it reacts with and neutralises excess stomach acid, while paracetamol (G) relieves pain and fever by a different action and does not neutralise acid; (3) the adult paracetamol maximum is 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g in 24 hours and more can damage the liver; (4) salt (A) and sugar (H) dissolve and cannot be filtered out, which matters in food and sugar industries such as Mumias and Nzoia; (5) sulphur (D) burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell (sulphur dioxide), so its use needs care.
slo.skills: Learners will: develop and use models (revise class model v1 to v2); obtain, evaluate and communicate information (brainstorm and share industry links); construct explanations using tray evidence; analyse and interpret data (calculate 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g); collaborate and communicate in groups (KICD core competencies: Communication and Collaboration; Citizenship).
slo.attitudes: Value: Respect. Learners show acceptance by appreciating the opinion of each group member as they discuss how chemistry is used in different industries. Learners appreciate the importance of chemistry in Kenya and adopt a responsible attitude to medicines and chemicals. PCIs: Life skills (safety and security); Health Promotion Issues (drug and substance use) through safe dosage; Socio-Economic and Environmental issues (consumer protection).
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Questions: (1) How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? (2) Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? (3) Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding especially those that are man-made the way they are? Lesson focus: How does knowing the properties of substances like A-H help Kenyan industries make useful products, and how do we use them safely?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 gave the class model v1 (classifying A-H as elements, compounds or mixtures) and Lesson 5 taught the five branches of chemistry (organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, biochemistry). Lesson 6 moves from asking what chemistry is to asking why it matters: learners connect tray evidence to real Kenyan industries and revise the model to v2. Lesson 7 will use these industries to explore careers, Lesson 8 will examine product labels, and Lesson 9 will study drugs and substance abuse.
slo.safetyNotes: No tasting of any substance A-H or any product. Goggles on for any demonstration. Sulphur (D) burning is a teacher-only demonstration, in a well-ventilated space or near an open window, with a very small amount in a deflagrating spoon; learners stand back and do not inhale the sharp choking sulphur dioxide fumes. Learners with asthma sit near the door. Tablets F and G are never swallowed in class and are handled as lab materials only. Wash hands after handling. Discuss medicines only as information: never give children adult doses and always follow the label or a health worker's advice.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns to the Kisumu tray (A salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar) and asks: 'If these eight ordinary things behave so differently, who in Kenya uses these differences, and why?' Learners predict which industries rely on each property, then gather evidence from short Kenyan industry cards (Kericho tea, Magadi soda ash, Mumias/Nzoia sugar, KenGen Olkaria geothermal, Kenya Pipeline, Nairobi pharmaceutical manufacturers, nyama choma and ugali) and a quick teacher-led sulphur demonstration. They explain how each industry uses properties, work out the safe paracetamol maximum (8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours), add new questions to the Driving Question Board, and revise model v1 to v2 by adding an 'Industries and uses' layer and a 'Safety' layer. This advances the driving question about how properties help chemists make medicines, foods and other products and how to use them safely.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 12 minutes) Groups of four (e.g. Group 1: Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir) look at their tray A-H and a list of nine industries: agriculture, pharmaceutical, medicine, manufacturing, entertainment, nuclear, food, sports and energy. Individually they write for 2 minutes: 'Which industry do you think uses the property of one tray substance? Choose at least three substances.' Example prompts: salt and sugar dissolving and food; sulphur burning and energy or manufacturing; the antacid reacting with acid and medicine. Groups then agree on one prediction and record it on a Predict card: 'We think ___ industry uses ___ because ___.' They also predict: 'Why might the same chemical be both useful and dangerous?'
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up tray A-H and say: 'Last time we met the five branches. Today we ask: who in Kenya depends on the differences we saw at this tray?' Read the nine industries aloud. Say: 'Write silently first. There are no wrong predictions today.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after the question 'Which industry might use the way salt and sugar dissolve?' before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups (not volunteers) to share one prediction; ask a different learner to restate each: 'Who can say that in your own words?' Say: 'Respect: listen to every idea in your group before choosing one.' Circulate and note common ideas; do not correct yet. Post two or three predictions on the board under the heading 'Our v1 ideas about use'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-and-Record with individual silent writing before group talk (Think-Write-Pair-Share). Making private ideas visible lets every learner commit to a prediction, which creates a reason to look for evidence and gives a baseline for noticing how thinking changes. Connecting to Lesson 3's model v1 reminds learners the model so far only classifies A-H.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each learner writes at least three substance-industry links independently within the 2 minutes; check Predict cards for a property named (e.g. dissolves, burns, reacts with acid) rather than only an industry name; tally on a checklist how many groups link a property to a use. Look for learners who invite every member's idea (Respect indicator).

framework.learnerExperience: (About 25 minutes) Learners rotate through three evidence stations (8 minutes each) in their groups. STATION 1 - Industry cards: short Kenyan cards on agriculture (fertilisers and soil testing for Kericho tea), manufacturing (Magadi soda ash and detergents), food (Mumias/Nzoia sugar: sugar H dissolves, and salt A as a preservative and flavour for nyama choma and ugali), energy (KenGen geothermal at Olkaria and Kenya Pipeline fuels), sports (energy drinks and sports-injury creams), entertainment (colours in fireworks and stage lighting), and nuclear chemistry (radioisotopes used in hospitals and in research). Learners fill a table: Industry | Substance or property from tray | How chemistry helps. STATION 2 - Medicine facts card: antacid (F) neutralises excess stomach acid, relieving heartburn; paracetamol (G) relieves pain and fever and does not neutralise acid; adult label: 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours. Learners calculate 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g and record: 'More than this can damage the liver.' They re-observe F fizzing in dilute vinegar and G giving no fizz (teacher-prepared samples). Learners also read that antacid taken too often can cause constipation or diarrhoea. STATION 3 - Teacher-led demonstration (watched from a safe distance, goggles on): a very small amount of sulphur (D) melts and burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell (sulphur dioxide). Learners record what they see and smell from a distance, and recall that sand (C) did not change when heated, whereas sulphur burns. They link this to manufacturing and energy industries that use burning reactions carefully.
framework.teacherMoves: Before stations say: 'You are chemists collecting evidence. Every claim needs a piece of evidence from the tray or the card.' Set a 8-minute timer per station. At Station 2 ask: 'Which tablet works by reacting with acid? How do you know from the fizz?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Ask: 'If a learner takes 10 tablets of 500 mg in one day, how many mg is that and how does it compare to 4000 mg?' (10 x 500 = 5000 mg, which is 1000 mg over the limit). Cold-call 3 groups to share their calculation. For the sulphur demonstration, put on goggles, use a tiny amount in a deflagrating spoon by an open window, and say: 'Stay behind the line. Do not sniff directly. What do you notice about the flame and smell?' Cold-call 2 learners to describe. Remind: 'Never taste. Never give a child an adult dose.' Circulate to make sure every learner records in their own notebook.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Table with Claim-Evidence Linking (stations rotation). Learners connect each industry use to a measurable property they have already observed on the tray (dissolving, magnetism, melting, burning, reaction with acid), turning abstract 'importance of chemistry' into specific, testable links. Repeated retrieval of observations from Lessons 2-3 deepens understanding of properties as the reason for uses.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the evidence tables: at least 6 of 9 industries filled with a named substance or property. Listen for correct statements such as 'The antacid fizzes in vinegar because it reacts with acid' and 'Paracetamol did not fizz so it does not neutralise acid'. Check the calculation 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g is correct and units are written. Note who records the sulphur observations (blue flame, sharp choking smell) accurately.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 18 minutes) Each group writes a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) paragraph answering: 'How does knowing the properties of substances help Kenyan industries make useful products and keep people safe?' They must use at least three tray substances (e.g. F and G for medicine; A and H for food; D for burning and energy; E and C for separation and manufacturing) and at least two industries. Groups include the idea that the antacid works because it reacts with and neutralises acid, while paracetamol relieves pain and fever by a different action, and that too much of either is harmful. Then each group joins another group in a Gallery Swap: they read the neighbouring CER and give one 'star' (a strong point) and one 'wish' (a missing link), using respectful language. Finally, as a class, learners help Wanjiru answer: 'Why does the antacid relieve heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain?' using the evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one sentence stem on the board: 'Claim: ___ industry uses the property of ___. Evidence: In our tray, ___. Reasoning: This matters because ___.' Say: 'Use at least one number or observation from our tray, such as 4 g or the blue flame.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What would go wrong if a pharmacist did not know that paracetamol is harmful above 4 g in 24 hours?' Cold-call 4 learners from different groups during the whole-class debrief; ask each: 'What evidence supports that?' Prompt for respect: 'How did your partner's idea change yours?' Ask: 'Salt A and sugar H both dissolve. How does that help a food or sugar factory such as Mumias or Nzoia?' Probe: 'Why can we not filter out dissolved sugar?' (it needs evaporation). Correct any misconception that all medicines work the same way, that more medicine means faster relief, or that 'natural' means safe. Do not re-teach branch definitions; ask learners to name which branch (from Lesson 5) each example belongs to, e.g. biochemistry for how the drug acts in the body.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Gallery Swap peer feedback. Writing CER forces learners to connect industry uses to observed properties and quantitative data, while peer star-and-wish feedback exposes gaps and builds collaboration and Respect. Linking to the branches from Lesson 5 shows how different parts of chemistry combine in real industries.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 3-point rubric on each CER: (1) names a correct industry use, (2) cites tray evidence (observation or number), (3) explains reasoning using a property. Look for correct statement that F reacts with and neutralises acid and G does not; correct use of 4 g maximum; correct link 'dissolves so cannot be filtered' for A and H. Note respectful, specific peer comments on swap sheets. Identify groups needing support for the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 10 minutes) Learners revisit the class DQB. In their groups they review the existing questions (e.g. Why do powders behave so differently? Why can some mixtures be separated and others not? How do properties help make medicines?). Each group (a) places a green sticky note next to one question they can now partly answer, writing the evidence (e.g. 'Antacid F reacts with acid so it relieves heartburn'), and (b) writes one new question on a yellow note arising from today, such as: 'How are medicines for chronic diseases developed?', 'Do substances in other countries have the same properties and uses?', 'Why are detergents and food products made the way they are?' or 'How do we know a medicine is safe?'. Groups place notes on the DQB under headings: Answered so far / New questions. The class picks two questions to follow into Lesson 7 (careers) and Lesson 8 (labels).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board is a record of our thinking. Which of our questions have we moved forward today?' Give each group 3 minutes to decide. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking: 'Which new question do you think a chemist working in a Nairobi pharmaceutical company would ask?' Cold-call 3 groups to read their new question and explain why it matters. Group similar questions together and link them to the KICD key inquiry questions. Say: 'Careers and labels are coming next, so keep these questions in mind.' Ensure every group has placed at least one answered and one new question.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Tracking. Visibly sorting questions into answered and new shows progress, shows that science is an ongoing process of asking questions, and gives learners ownership of the unit direction. Connecting to KICD inquiry questions keeps the unit coherent.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group has placed at least one green note supported by tray or industry evidence and one new question. Look for questions that move beyond recall (why/how) and for any link to safety. Note which questions refer to chronic-disease medicines or product design, to plan Lessons 7-9.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 15 minutes) Learners look at the class model v1 from Lesson 3 (classification of A-H into elements, compounds and mixtures). In groups they propose what to add so the model also explains why chemistry is important. As a class they build model v2 with two new layers: (1) 'Industries and uses' layer: arrows from properties (dissolves, magnetic, melts, burns, reacts with acid) to industries (food: A and H; agriculture; manufacturing: soda ash from Magadi; energy: Olkaria and Kenya Pipeline; medicine and pharmaceutical: F and G; sports; entertainment; nuclear), and (2) 'Safety' layer: arrows showing labels, correct dosage (maximum 4 g paracetamol in 24 hours), avoiding substance misuse and careful handling of sulphur burning. Each group draws a mini-version in their notebook and writes a 2-sentence caption answering the driving question: 'How do the different properties of substances help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely?' Groups mark what in v2 is still uncertain (e.g. how medicines for chronic diseases are developed).
framework.teacherMoves: Display v1 and say: 'v1 told us what the substances are made of. v2 must tell us what they are used for and how to stay safe. What should we add?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking suggestions. Cold-call 4 learners to propose one addition each and ask the class: 'Do we agree? What evidence supports it?' Draw the new layers with learner input, requiring each arrow to be justified by evidence from the tray or the industry cards. Ask: 'Which part of our model explains why the antacid and paracetamol are different?' and 'Where does safety belong?' Label the model 'v2 (Lesson 6)' and say: 'We will revise it again to reach the final model in Lesson 10.' Collect captions for review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (v1 to v2). Adding layers to an existing model shows how new evidence extends earlier ideas instead of replacing them, and justifying every arrow with evidence builds the habit of linking claims to data. Marking uncertainties creates a bridge to later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each mini-model for: (1) properties linked to at least four industries, (2) a safety layer that includes the 4 g paracetamol limit and avoiding misuse, (3) an evidence-based caption answering the driving question. Look for learners who can explain at least one arrow to a peer. Identify any misconception (e.g. that antacid and paracetamol do the same job) for follow-up in Lesson 8 and 9.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Could learners link at least three tray substances to specific industries using a property as evidence? (2) Did every learner correctly calculate 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g and explain why exceeding it is dangerous? (3) Did learners explain that the antacid (F) reacts with and neutralises acid while paracetamol (G) acts on pain and fever differently? (4) Which industry examples were unfamiliar, and how can I add local context (e.g. a nearby factory or farm in Kisumu) next time? (5) Did all voices contribute respectfully, and who did I not hear from? (6) How well did model v2 capture both uses and safety, and what do learners still wonder about for careers (Lesson 7) and labels (Lesson 8)? Note any safety issues during the sulphur demonstration and plan improvements.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Record what you observed: the properties of A-H (salt and sugar dissolve; sand and iron do not; iron is pulled by a magnet; sulphur melts and burns with a blue flame and sharp choking smell; F fizzes in dilute vinegar but G does not), and the Kenyan industry examples you studied.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Record what you learned: chemistry is important in agriculture, pharmaceutical, medicine, manufacturing, entertainment, nuclear, food, sports and energy industries because industries choose, separate and make materials using properties; the antacid neutralises acid, paracetamol relieves pain and fever, and the adult maximum is 8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Explain how this helps answer the driving question: use evidence from the tray and at least two industries to explain how properties help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how labels, correct dosage and avoiding substance misuse keep people safe. Describe what you added to model v2.

LESSONS.title: Careers in Chemistry: Who Works with the Kisumu Tray Substances, and Who Gets to Choose?
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 80 minutes is recommended if digital search is used)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: careers in chemistry, pharmacist, analytical chemist, quality control, chemical engineer, gender stereotypes, career choice, Pharmacy and Poisons Board, KEBS, plenary presentation

slo.purpose: Learners search print and digital media for careers related to Chemistry, link each career to the Kisumu tray evidence (antacid F, paracetamol G and the separation of mixture M), examine how gender stereotypes influence career choices, and present findings in plenary.
slo.knowledge: Chemistry careers (for example pharmacist, analytical chemist, quality control officer, chemical engineer, food technologist, laboratory technician, drug inspector, geothermal chemist) each use the properties of substances (solubility, magnetism, melting point, reaction with acid) that learners saw in the tray. A gender stereotype is a fixed idea about what girls or boys can or should do; it can limit career choice but does not change who can do chemistry.
slo.skills: Searching for information in print and electronic media; evaluating sources; collaborating in groups; presenting findings in plenary; constructing evidence-based explanations (NGSS SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information; Engaging in Argument from Evidence).
slo.attitudes: Respect (KICD value): the learner shows acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each member in group discussion. Self-efficacy: confidence in presenting findings. Citizenship: critical and constructive dialogue. Openness to careers in chemistry regardless of gender.
slo.keyInquiry: How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? Who are the people that do this work, and what properties of substances do they use? (KICD key inquiry 1, with a link to key inquiry 3 on how products are made.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 5 and 6 gave us the branches of chemistry and the industries that use chemistry in Kenya. Lesson 7 asks who works in those branches and industries and what they do with the properties we found in the tray. It advances the driving question by showing that people with different careers use properties to make medicines, separate mixtures and keep products safe. It also prepares Lesson 8 (quality control and labels) and Lesson 9 (dosage and drugs).
slo.safetyNotes: No new heating or chemical tests. Trays A-H may be displayed sealed and must not be tasted; tablets F and G stay in their packets as props. Learners with devices use only school-approved or offline resources; the teacher supervises searches. Treat all learner opinions respectfully; no ridiculing of any learner's career dreams. Hands washed if trays were handled.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng brings the Group 1 tray (A salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar) and mixture M back to the front. She asks: 'Someone had to decide that F relieves heartburn and G does not, and someone had to separate and check what is in a product. Who are these people?' Learners predict careers, then research in groups from print (career booklets, newspapers, textbooks) and offline or digital resources, matching each career to a tray property. Next they examine a short set of career profiles and survey data to discuss how gender stereotypes shape choices, and each group presents in plenary. The class adds new questions to the DQB and records how careers help answer the driving question, in readiness for revising the model in Lesson 10.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the tray (A-H) and mixture M displayed in Group 1's setup. In their notebooks they individually write: (1) three jobs in which a person might use the properties of F antacid or G paracetamol or the separation of mixture M (magnet, filtration, evaporation); (2) one prediction: 'Do you think more men or more women work as chemists in Kenya? Why?' Then they share in groups of four (like Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir) and agree on a group list of five possible careers.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up tablet packets F and G and say: 'Wanjiru asked why the antacid relieves heartburn but paracetamol relieves pain. Who in Kisumu or Nairobi might answer that question for a living?' Give 1 minute silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before any hands go up. Say: 'Turn to your group; every voice must be heard, and we thank each person for their idea.' Cold-call 4 groups (not volunteers) to give one career each, and record on the board without correcting. Ask one neutral question: 'What made you think of that job?' Do not comment on the gender prediction yet; just record the class tally on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with a recorded prediction. Writing alone first activates prior knowledge from Lessons 5 and 6 (branches and industries) and exposes learners' initial ideas, including stereotypes, so that they can be compared with evidence later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: each learner has written three jobs and one reasoned prediction; at least 6 of 8 groups name a career linked to medicine or testing (for example pharmacist, laboratory technician); groups give reasons that mention a property or an industry from Lesson 6. Note learners who give gendered reasons (for example 'chemistry is for boys') for use in the Explain phase, without naming them.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups receive a Career Research Card and spend about 15 minutes gathering evidence from print (career booklets, textbooks, newspaper cut-outs, KCSE career guides) and, where available, school-approved digital sources or offline resource files. Each group researches three careers: (a) pharmacist or pharmaceutical scientist (relates to F and G and the Pharmacy and Poisons Board), (b) analytical chemist or laboratory technician (relates to separating mixture M: magnet, filtration, evaporation, with 2.9 g, 2.8 g and 2.7 g recovered and 0.6 g lost out of 9 g), (c) one free choice such as quality control officer at KEBS, food technologist (Mumias/Nzoia sugar, Kericho tea), chemical engineer (Magadi soda ash), geothermal chemist (KenGen, Olkaria). For each, they fill a table: career, what the person does, which tray property or separation method is used, branch of chemistry from Lesson 5, and one example of a Kenyan employer. Roles in the group: reader, recorder, searcher, presenter, rotated. Second, groups read three short career profiles (for example a woman analytical chemist in a Nairobi pharmaceutical company and a man food technologist) supplied by the teacher as examples, and note any statement that shows a stereotype.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with the question: 'Which property from our tray does this person use, and how do you know?' Prompt: 'Show me the line in your source that says so.' For groups with only digital sources, ask: 'Who wrote this and can we trust it? What is a second source?' Stop the whole class at 8 minutes: 'Pens down. Recorders, read one row aloud.' Use 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME after asking: 'Is the job described only for men or only for women, or does the source just say a person?' Cold-call 3 groups for one piece of evidence each. Remind: 'Appreciate each person's contribution; use the phrase "I agree with... because..." or "I see it differently because..."'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence table with source evaluation (Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information). Linking each career to a tray property or separation step makes the abstract job concrete and shows that careers apply the same properties that explain the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the tables: each group has three careers with a named property or separation step (for example 'filtration removes sand C; analytical chemist checks purity') and a branch; at least one group notes that the filtrate evaporation recovers salt A (2.7 g). Observe collaboration: all four learners contribute to the table, roles rotated, and respectful phrases are used. Collect any digital-literacy problems such as accepting the first search result without checking.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their evidence to explain two ideas in groups, then in class. First: 'How does a career in pharmaceutical or analytical chemistry help us answer why F relieves heartburn and G relieves pain, and why too much of either is harmful?' They write a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph using MEDICINE FACTS: antacid neutralises excess stomach acid; paracetamol relieves pain and fever and does not neutralise acid; adult paracetamol maximum is 8 tablets of 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g in 24 hours; more can damage the liver. Second: they compare their Predict-phase gender tally with the career profiles and discuss 'What is a gender stereotype? How might it stop a girl or a boy from choosing chemistry? What does the evidence show about who can do these jobs?' Groups then prepare a 2-minute plenary presentation with one poster sheet and present, with one group member from each group speaking and a different member answering questions.
framework.teacherMoves: Model a sentence frame on the board: 'A [career] uses [property] to [action], which helps [people or product].' Ask: 'Why is it not enough for a pharmacist to know that F fizzes in vinegar?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Then: 'What do labels and dosage tell us, and who writes and checks them?' (Preview of Lesson 8, not taught here.) For stereotypes, define: 'A gender stereotype is a fixed idea about what girls or boys should do.' Ask: 'Where do we see these ideas in Kisumu, in the media, in families?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners from different groups. Say: 'We disagree with ideas, never with people.' During plenary, cold-call 2 listeners per presentation to restate one point and ask: 'What evidence supports that?' Do not allow stereotypes to be stated as facts; redirect: 'What evidence do we have for that?' Ensure girls and boys both speak.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning plus Structured Academic Controversy-style discussion (Engaging in Argument from Evidence). CER ties careers to the tray data and medicine facts; the stereotype discussion has learners test a claim against evidence from profiles and their own tally, building critical and constructive dialogue and self-efficacy.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for CER paragraphs that include a claim, at least two pieces of evidence (for example 'F fizzes in vinegar, so it reacts with acid' and '8 x 500 mg = 4 g maximum') and reasoning linking to a career. In the stereotype discussion, look for learners who define a stereotype in their own words, give a reason that is evidence-based, and show respect by building on another's idea. In plenary, check that presenters speak clearly and that at least 6 of 8 groups present accurate property-career links. Note any learner still holding 'chemistry is for boys/girls' and plan a follow-up conversation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB. Each group writes on sticky notes (1) one thing the careers research helped answer about the driving question, placed under 'We have evidence for...', and (2) one new question, for example 'How long does it take to develop a medicine?' or 'What subjects do I need to become a pharmacist in Kenya?' They place notes on the DQB, moving or linking earlier questions such as Wanjiru's about F and G.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which earlier question can a career now help answer?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to move or connect a question and explain why. Ask: 'Which of our questions needs a person with a different job, such as a drug inspector or quality control officer?' Mark questions about labels, quality marks and drug dosage with a star: 'We will return to these in Lessons 8 and 9.' Keep note of questions for the model revision.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery sort of the DQB. Sorting questions into answered, partly answered and new makes learning visible, keeps the phenomenon at the centre and tells learners where the storyline goes next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sticky notes: each group posted one evidence note and one new question; at least half the new questions link to a career or to product safety; learners can justify where they placed a note. Observe whether learners connect Wanjiru's question to pharmaceutical and analytical roles.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their personal copy of the class model v2 from Lesson 6 and add a section titled 'People who use properties'. With a drawing or flow chart they show how a pharmacist or pharmaceutical scientist, an analytical chemist or technician and a quality control officer connect the properties of A-H (solubility, magnetism, melting point, reaction with acid) to making, separating and checking products such as F antacid and G paracetamol. They label where safety (dosage, label, avoiding substance misuse) fits. The model remains a v2 draft with additions marked in a different colour; it will be finalised in Lesson 10.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add a new part to your model: the people. Arrows should show property, then job, then product or safety.' Give 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME before groups begin drawing. Circulate and ask: 'Where does the 0.6 g loss in mixture M matter for an analytical chemist?' and 'Where in your model does a person keep someone safe from too much paracetamol?' Cold-call 3 groups to explain one arrow. Ask: 'Does your model show that a career is open to everyone, whatever their gender?' Collect models for the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision with added components. Adding people and decisions to the property-based model shows that chemistry knowledge is applied by humans, which helps learners build towards a full answer to the driving question and a view of themselves in chemistry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models with at least three labelled arrows linking a property or separation step to a career and a product or safety outcome (for example 'magnet removes iron E: lab technician checks purity'); correct use of tray letters and names; revisions marked in a new colour. Exit ticket: 'Name one career and the tray property it uses.' Success: at least 80% of learners name a matched pair.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners offered stereotypes, and were they challenged with evidence rather than embarrassed? Did every group find a clear link between a career and a property from the tray (F, G or mixture M)? Were all four group members, including quieter learners, speaking during research and presentation? Which sources did learners trust without checking, and how will I teach source evaluation next time? Which DQB questions about labels and dosage should open Lesson 8? Which learners need support to see themselves in chemistry careers?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that careers such as pharmacist, analytical chemist, laboratory technician and quality control officer use the properties of substances we saw in the tray: F antacid reacts with acid, G paracetamol does not, and mixture M was separated by magnet, filtration and evaporation (2.9 g, 2.8 g and 2.7 g recovered out of 9 g).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that chemistry offers many careers in medicine, industry and testing, and that gender stereotypes are fixed ideas that can wrongly limit who chooses these careers.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that people in chemistry careers use properties to make, separate and check products such as medicines, and that safety through labels and correct dosage matters, and that girls and boys can both choose these careers; this adds to our answer to the driving question.

LESSONS.title: Consumer Protection and Product Labels: Reading the Story a Label Tells
LESSONS.aresKeywords: label, quality mark, KEBS Diamond Mark, expiry date, ingredients, preservative, caution, dosage, consumer protection, Pharmacy and Poisons Board

slo.purpose: Learners read and interpret labels on manufactured products (including the paracetamol 500 mg label from the Kisumu tray) to identify quality marks, expiry dates, ingredients and preservatives, nutritional information and caution messages, and explain how this information protects consumers.
slo.knowledge: A label is the chemist's and manufacturer's message to the consumer. The KEBS Diamond Mark shows a product has met quality standards. The expiry date shows when a product may no longer be safe or effective. Ingredients and preservatives show what a product is made of. Caution messages and dosage instructions prevent harm. The paracetamol label (adult: 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets = 4000 mg = 4 g in 24 hours) uses the properties of substance G to keep people safe, because more than this can damage the liver. Antacid F also carries a label: taking it too often can upset the body's salts and cause constipation or diarrhoea. Children must not be given adult doses.
slo.skills: Observing and recording information from labels; asking questions (SEP 1); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (SEP 8); using mathematics to check dosage (8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g) (SEP 5); constructing explanations (SEP 6); developing and using models (SEP 2).
slo.attitudes: Respect: learners show acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each member as they discuss label information in groups. Learners develop a habit of reading labels before buying or using any product. Citizenship: learners recognise the consumer's right to information on drug prescription, substance use and side effects.
slo.keyInquiry: Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding, especially those that are man-made, the way they are, and how does the information on their labels help consumers use them safely?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 6 showed how chemistry is used in industries and products, and Lesson 7 introduced careers in chemistry. This lesson moves from who makes products to how consumers are protected, by reading labels. Learners see that the properties studied in Lessons 1 to 3 (for example, paracetamol G and antacid F) are communicated through labels, and that quality control chemists check them. It prepares Lesson 9 (drugs, prescription, dosage and substance abuse), where dosage information is explored in depth.
slo.safetyNotes: No tasting or smelling of any product or tablet. Tablets F and G remain sealed or are handled only with clean hands and are NOT swallowed. Use empty, clean, washed containers for food and detergent samples. Do not open detergents or chemical products. Wash hands after the activity. Do not give anyone medicines in class. Wear goggles only if any demonstration with the tray is repeated. Explain that expired medicines are returned to a pharmacy or health facility, not thrown away or shared.

LESSONS.overview: Otieno comes to class from his family's kiosk with a worrying story: a customer asked for paracetamol (like tablet G on Mrs Achieng's Kisumu tray) and wanted to give an adult dose to a small child. Learners predict what a label should tell a buyer, then examine sample containers (a paracetamol 500 mg box, an antacid pack, a packet of maize flour, a juice carton and a detergent bottle, all empty or sealed) for the KEBS Diamond Mark, expiry date, ingredients and preservatives, nutritional information and cautions. They explain how each label item protects consumers, check the maximum paracetamol dose (8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours), add new questions to the Driving Question Board, and revisit the class model (v2) to note where labels fit in. The lesson advances the driving question by showing how knowledge of properties is turned into safe use.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners listen to Otieno's kiosk scenario: a customer wants to buy paracetamol and give an adult dose to a small child, and another customer asks if a packet of old biscuits is still fine. In Group 1 (Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir) and the other 7 groups, learners individually write in their notebooks: (1) three things they think a label on a medicine or food must tell the buyer, and (2) a prediction: 'If a customer reads only the label on tablet G (paracetamol 500 mg), what will they know about how to use it safely?' Groups then share and combine their predictions on a group chart under the headings 'Must be on a label' and 'Why it matters'. Learners link back to the Kisumu tray: G and F look like ordinary tablets, so how would a person know which one to use and how many?
framework.teacherMoves: Greet learners and say: 'Today we leave the tray for a moment and look at what the shopkeeper sells. Otieno, tell us about your kiosk.' Invite Otieno to share the story briefly (2 minutes). Ask: 'Tablet G and tablet F look like simple white tablets. How would a buyer know what each one is for and how much to take?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Give 3 minutes of silent individual writing, then 4 minutes of group sharing. Cold-call 4 learners (one from each of 4 different groups) to read one 'must be on a label' item, and write all items on the board without correcting yet. Ask: 'What would happen if a label had no expiry date?' Cold-call 2 more learners. Circulate and note which groups mention quality marks, dosage and cautions, and which mention only the product name.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior knowledge through individual-then-group prediction (Think-Write-Share). Making predictions visible on the board builds understanding because learners commit to ideas that they will test against real labels in the Observe Phase, which creates a need to know and a clear comparison point for later revision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) At least 6 of 8 groups list three or more label items on their chart. (2) Count how many learners mention dosage or caution (target: at least half of the class). (3) Note learners who mention expiry date or the KEBS Diamond Mark without prompting. (4) Individual notebook check: each learner has written a prediction about tablet G with a reason. Learners with only the product name need a prompt: 'What would a mother need to know to give this to her child safely?'

framework.learnerExperience: Each of the 8 groups receives a label kit of clean, empty or sealed containers: a paracetamol 500 mg box (tablet G), an antacid pack (tablet F), a maize flour packet (ugali), a bottled juice or milk carton, and a detergent bottle. A label observation table has these columns: Product | KEBS Diamond Mark? | Expiry date | Ingredients / preservatives | Nutritional information | Caution or dose message. Learners take roles (reader, recorder, checker, reporter), rotate the roles after 2 products, and use a hand lens or magnifying glass where needed. They record exactly what is written, for example the paracetamol label: adult dose 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours, and a warning that more can damage the liver. They note that the antacid label warns about taking it too often (can cause constipation or diarrhoea) and advises following the label or a health worker's advice. They compare food labels (maize flour, juice) which list ingredients, preservatives and nutritional information with the medicine labels, which list active ingredient, dose and cautions. Learners also spot where a product has NO mark or date and record this as 'missing information'.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute kits and say: 'You are consumer protection inspectors from the Kenya Bureau of Standards. Read exactly what is printed. Do not taste, smell or open anything.' Show the KEBS Diamond Mark on an enlarged poster or sample. Remind learners of the rule: 'No tasting, no swallowing tablets, wash hands afterwards.' Circulate for 15 minutes and ask: 'Where on the pack did you find the expiry date? What does the date tell you that your eyes cannot?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask groups: 'What does the caution on the paracetamol box tell you about the property of substance G in the body?' Cold-call 3 recorders to report one finding they found surprising. Prompt rotation of roles at the 7 minute mark. For groups that finish early: 'Find a product with a preservative and tell me what you think it prevents.' For learners who need support, give a labelled diagram of a sample label with arrows. Collect observations on a class table on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with a label observation table (Obtaining information, SEP 8). Using the same table headings for every product allows patterns to emerge across foods, detergents and medicines, so learners can see that different product types carry different information because of different risks.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group's table has at least 4 products with at least 4 of the 6 columns completed accurately. (2) Learners correctly copy the paracetamol dose (1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours). (3) Learners distinguish preservatives from active ingredients when asked. (4) At least 6 groups record at least one case of missing or unclear information. (5) Roles were rotated and every learner recorded or read at least once; note any learner not participating.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups use their label tables to explain how each label item protects consumers. Individually, then in groups, learners complete a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement: 'Claim: Labels protect consumers. Evidence: (from our table). Reasoning: (why this item matters).' Each group chooses one item (quality mark, expiry date, ingredients and preservatives, nutritional information, or cautions) and explains it using the paracetamol label as a worked case. They calculate the daily maximum: 8 tablets x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g, and answer Otieno's kiosk question: 'A customer wants to give a small child 2 tablets of 500 mg. Why is this unsafe even though it is within the adult dose?' (Children must not be given adult doses.) They also explain why antacid F and paracetamol G need different labels (antacid neutralises excess stomach acid to relieve heartburn; paracetamol relieves pain and fever) and what could go wrong if the two are confused. Learners then discuss in groups how a quality control chemist (Lesson 7) would check that a batch of tablets in a Nairobi factory matches its label. Respect is practised: each learner must acknowledge one idea from a groupmate before adding their own.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now we move from reading to explaining. A label is evidence. What does your evidence say?' Model one CER on the board with the expiry date. Give 6 minutes for group writing. Circulate and ask: 'How do you know that 4 g is the limit? Show me the calculation.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Probe: 'If a label says maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours, what do you think happens if someone takes 12?' (can damage the liver). Ask: 'Why does the label say more than the dose can damage the liver, and not just it is wasteful?' Cold-call 4 groups (one reporter each) to present their CER in 1 minute. After each, ask the class: 'Who can add to or challenge this claim using the evidence on your own table?' Cold-call 3 more learners. Reinforce respect by saying: 'Start your response with: I agree with ... because ...'. Clarify that the KEBS Diamond Mark shows the product met a standard and the Pharmacy and Poisons Board regulates medicines in Kenya. Do not teach dosage and drug abuse in depth, as these belong to Lesson 9: say 'We will study this more deeply in the next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer critique (SEP 6, Constructing Explanations, and SEP 7, Engaging in argument from evidence). CER builds understanding because learners must tie each statement to their own label data and explain why the evidence supports it, moving from copying text to understanding purpose. Peer critique makes reasoning visible and corrects errors.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group CER contains a claim, at least one specific piece of evidence from the table, and a reason linking to consumer safety. (2) Learners correctly calculate 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g. (3) At least 5 of 8 groups state that adult doses should not be given to children. (4) Learners can state that antacid F neutralises acid and paracetamol G relieves pain and fever, and that both are harmful in excess. (5) Learners use respectful phrases when responding to peers (count the instances). Misconception check: a learner who says that a product without an expiry date is safe forever needs more guidance.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the driving question: 'How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely?' Each group writes one 'We now know...' sticky note from today's label evidence (for example: 'The label on G tells us the maximum is 4 g in 24 hours because more can damage the liver') and one new 'We still wonder...' question (for example: 'How do chemists test that the tablets contain exactly 500 mg?' or 'Why do some foods need preservatives and others do not?'). They place notes next to the KICD key inquiry question: 'Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding, especially those that are man-made, the way they are?' The class also sorts questions into those that can be answered in Lesson 9 (drugs, prescription, dosage, substance abuse) and Lesson 10 (safe and healthy learning environment, final model). Wanjiru's earlier question about why the antacid and paracetamol differ is revisited and marked with what the labels add.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board is growing. Which of our earlier questions did the labels help to answer?' Point to Wanjiru's question about why the antacid relieves heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Give groups 3 minutes to write one 'now know' and one 'still wonder' sticky note. Cold-call 4 groups to read their notes aloud and place them on the board. Ask: 'Which of these new questions will Lesson 9 help us answer?' Cold-call 2 learners to sort the questions. Mark any answered questions with a tick and the evidence source (for example, 'Label table, Lesson 8'). Praise questions that ask how or why, and rephrase yes/no questions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a tool for tracking growing understanding and ownership of learning. Linking each note to evidence and to the next lesson helps learners see learning as a connected storyline, and learner-generated questions keep curiosity and purpose high.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) All 8 groups post one 'now know' statement backed by label evidence. (2) At least 6 groups post a new, testable or researchable question. (3) Learners correctly link at least one note to the driving question or a KICD key inquiry question. (4) Check that 'now know' statements do not claim more than the evidence shows (for example, 'all medicines are safe if the label is present' is incorrect).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class model, currently at version 2 (from Lesson 6), which links properties of substances A-H to their uses in industries. In groups, they add a new layer, 'Labels and consumer protection', as a section on the model: arrows from properties (for example, solubility, burning, reaction with acid) to product uses (antacid F, paracetamol G, food products like sugar H and salt A) to label information (quality mark, expiry date, ingredients and preservatives, dose, caution) to safe use by the consumer. They add Otieno's kiosk as a point where the consumer meets the product, and a quality control chemist as the person who checks that products match their labels. Each group draws or adds the revision on a model chart and records a short caption: 'One thing we added to the model today and why.' Learners also annotate where they are still unsure, to be revisited in Lesson 9 and in the final model in Lesson 10.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now answer a new part of the driving question: how do we use these products safely? Where do labels fit?' Display model v2. Give 8 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'How does the label connect the property of substance G to a safe amount for a person?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'What is missing from our model if a customer cannot read the label?' Cold-call 3 groups to explain one new arrow or box. Ask 2 other learners to say whether the addition makes sense using evidence. Do not yet create the final model; say: 'This is a working revision. In Lesson 9 we add drugs and misuse, and in Lesson 10 we finalise.' Close with the exit question: 'Name one label item you will check the next time you buy a product, and say why.' Take answers from 4 learners by cold-call.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Developing and revising models (SEP 2). Adding a new layer to an existing model builds understanding by showing how new evidence extends rather than replaces earlier ideas, and by connecting the science (properties) to real-world decisions (labels and safe use).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group's model includes at least three label items correctly connected to consumer safety. (2) The model links a property or substance from the tray (for example, G or F) to a label message. (3) At least 6 groups add the role of the quality control chemist or KEBS. (4) Exit responses name a specific label item and a valid reason (for example, 'I will check the expiry date because old medicine may not work or may be unsafe'). (5) Learners identify one remaining uncertainty for Lesson 9.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners read labels carefully, or only copy the product names? Which groups needed prompting to find the expiry date or caution? (2) Did learners correctly calculate 8 x 500 mg = 4 g and explain why it is the maximum, or did they just repeat the text? (3) How well did learners show Respect in group discussion, for example, acknowledging a groupmate's idea before adding their own? (4) Were any learners unable to read the labels because of language or print size, and how can you support them in Lesson 9? (5) Did the CER statements show a link between the properties of substances F and G and the safety information? (6) Which DQB questions will you carry into Lesson 9, and which learners should lead them? Keep a note of any learners who said that a medicine is safe because it is in a shop, and revisit this idea in Lesson 9.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed the labels on a paracetamol 500 mg box (G), an antacid pack (F), a maize flour packet, a juice carton and a detergent bottle. We found the KEBS Diamond Mark, expiry dates, ingredients and preservatives, nutritional information, and caution and dose messages, and we noticed where information was missing.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that labels protect consumers by giving information on quality, how long a product is safe to use, what it contains, and how to use it safely. The paracetamol label says adults take 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, with a maximum of 8 tablets (4000 mg = 4 g) in 24 hours, because more can damage the liver. Antacid taken too often can cause constipation or diarrhoea, and children must not be given adult doses.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Substances like the antacid (F) and paracetamol (G) have different properties and uses, so their labels give different instructions. Labels turn what chemists know about the properties of substances into safe-use messages for the consumer. This helps answer the driving question about how we use products safely, and prepares us to study drugs, dosage and substance abuse in Lesson 9.

LESSONS.title: Drugs and Substance Abuse: Why the Dose Makes the Difference
LESSONS.aresKeywords: drug, prescription, dosage, substance use, substance abuse, paracetamol, antacid, label, overdose, poster, Pharmacy and Poisons Board

slo.purpose: Learners use evidence from the Kisumu tray (antacid F and paracetamol G) to explain drug, prescription, dosage and substance use, and to examine the effects of drug and substance abuse in day-to-day life. They then design posters to sensitise peers and the community, advancing the driving question on how properties help chemists make medicines and how we use them safely.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to: (a) define drug, prescription, dosage and substance abuse using the class conventions; (b) explain that antacid F neutralises excess stomach acid while paracetamol G relieves pain and fever by a different action, and that both are harmful in excess; (c) calculate the paracetamol maximum of 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g in 24 hours; (d) describe the effects of antacid overuse (upset body salts, constipation or diarrhoea) and of paracetamol overdose (liver damage).
slo.skills: Making predictions; interpreting label data and doing simple calculations (mg to g); constructing explanations from evidence (NGSS SEP: Constructing Explanations); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information through a poster (NGSS SEP); collaborating in groups of four.
slo.attitudes: Respect: learners accept and value each member's ideas during group discussion (KICD value). Responsibility: learners advocate for safe medicine use and a healthy learning environment. Citizenship: learners recognise the consumer right to information on drug prescription, substance use and side effects.
slo.keyInquiry: How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? Why are food products, detergents and man-made things the way they are? (Lesson focus: How does what we know about the properties of a medicine help us decide a safe dose and avoid harm?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 8 taught how to read labels (quality mark, expiry date, ingredients, cautions) using the paracetamol 500 mg label and dose. Lesson 2 gave the evidence that substances have their own properties, including F reacting with acid and G not reacting. Lesson 9 uses that knowledge to answer Wanjiru's puzzle about why the antacid and paracetamol differ and why too much of either is dangerous. It turns the dosage information into community action through posters, preparing for Lesson 10, where learners finalise the model and consider rights and responsibilities for a safe school environment.
slo.safetyNotes: No tasting or swallowing of any substance in the lab. Goggles on for the demonstration. Teacher alone handles the vinegar-antacid demonstration; use the whole tablet F and dilute vinegar only. Tablets are never taken by learners. Handle the topic of substance abuse sensitively: do not ask learners to share personal or family experiences, and refer anyone who is worried to the school guidance and counselling teacher. Adult doses must never be given to children.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns to the Kisumu tray. Wanjiru asked earlier why antacid F relieves heartburn but paracetamol G relieves pain, and why too much of either is dangerous. Learners predict what happens in the body with each tablet, then gather evidence: a teacher-led demo of F fizzing in dilute vinegar (acid) while G does not (a Lesson 2 property), and a data card with the paracetamol label dose. They calculate 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g as the daily maximum, and examine the effects of antacid overuse. They define drug, prescription, dosage and substance abuse, explain why the dose matters, add to the Driving Question Board, and design a poster to sensitise peers and the community. The final step revises the class model with ideas about safe use.

framework.learnerExperience: Mrs Achieng holds up antacid tablet F and paracetamol tablet G from the Group 1 tray (Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir). Learners recall Wanjiru's puzzle. Individually, in their notebooks, they write predictions for 3 questions: (1) What do you think each tablet does inside the body? (2) Do you think F and G work in the same way? Why or why not? (3) What might happen if a person takes far more tablets than the label says? Then each group of four shares and records one group prediction on a sticky note, with each member's idea acknowledged (Respect).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last week Wanjiru asked why the antacid and the paracetamol are different. Today we find out, and we also find out how to use them safely. Write your own prediction first, in silence, for 2 minutes.' Then: 'Share with your group. Each person speaks once, and the group writes down every idea, even ones you disagree with.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Cold-call 3 learners from different groups: 'Tell us one thing your group predicted. Do not tell us whose idea it was, just the idea.' Accept all ideas without judging; write key predictions on the board under 'Our predictions'. Do not reveal the answers yet. Remind: no tasting, tablets stay on the tray.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with individual then group prediction. Writing predictions before evidence exposes prior ideas (for example, that all tablets 'just cure sickness' or that more tablets mean faster relief) so that evidence in the Observe Phase can confirm or challenge them. It links directly to the anchoring phenomenon, where F and G look similar but behave differently.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) every learner has a written prediction before group talk (scan the notebooks during the silent 2 minutes and count empty pages); (2) group sticky notes contain at least 2 ideas; (3) at least 3 of 8 groups mention that a larger amount could be harmful; (4) learners listen without interrupting while others speak. Note common misconceptions on the board: 'all medicines do the same thing', 'more is always better'.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (teacher demo, 5 minutes): Learners watch Mrs Achieng drop a whole antacid tablet F into dilute vinegar (acid) and a whole paracetamol tablet G into dilute vinegar, wearing goggles. F fizzes; G does not fizz. Learners recall from the Lesson 2 water test that F crumbles into a cloudy white suspension while G stays mostly intact and crumbles slowly. Part B (data card, 10 minutes): Each group receives a Data Card with the facts: (i) adult paracetamol label: 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours; (ii) paracetamol: more than the label can damage the liver; (iii) antacid: taken too often can upset the body's salts and cause constipation or diarrhoea; (iv) do not give children adult doses; (v) the Pharmacy and Poisons Board regulates medicines in Kenya. Learners complete a table: tablet, what it does, what happens in excess, and calculate the maximum daily mass of paracetamol: 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g. They also calculate how many tablets would be taken in 24 hours at 2 tablets every 4 hours (6 doses x 2 = 12 tablets, which is 6000 mg, more than the 4000 mg maximum) to see how easy it is to exceed the limit.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the demo say: 'Goggles on. Only I handle the vinegar and the tablets. Watch the surface of the liquid and tell me what you see, not what you think.' Drop F, then G in separate beakers. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then ask: 'What did you observe in the beaker with F? And with G?' Cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'Vinegar is an acid. What does the fizzing tell us about how F behaves with acid?' Guide: F reacts with acid, which is why it can neutralise excess stomach acid; G does not react, so it does not neutralise acid. During the data card activity circulate to every group and ask: 'Where did the 4000 mg come from? Show me the working.' and 'Why is 4000 mg the same as 4 g?' (1000 mg = 1 g). Prompt groups that reach 12 tablets: 'Does this follow the label? What does the label's maximum protect?' Remind them that this must never be tried and that only a health worker's advice or the label guides dosage.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence table with data interpretation (Analysing and Interpreting Data, NGSS SEP). Placing observations (fizzing or not), label numbers and effects in one table lets learners see patterns: the same property tested in Lesson 2 (reaction with acid) explains the medicine's action, and the dosage numbers explain the safety limits. The calculation turns an abstract warning into a concrete limit of 4 g in 24 hours.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that: (1) the table records F fizzes in vinegar and G does not; (2) at least 6 of 8 groups correctly get 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g; (3) learners convert mg to g correctly; (4) groups can state the effects of too much of each tablet (liver damage for paracetamol; upset body salts, constipation or diarrhoea for antacid); (5) learners use the words 'maximum' and 'label' in their explanations. Use a thumbs-up check: 'Show me thumbs up if you can explain why 12 tablets in a day is too many.' Tally the number of thumbs.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build a group explanation answering Wanjiru's puzzle in 4 to 5 sentences: (1) why the antacid relieves heartburn but paracetamol relieves pain, using the acid-reaction evidence; (2) why taking too much of either is dangerous, using the dose numbers. Then, using a class discussion, learners build definitions of the four key terms: drug (a substance that changes how the body works), prescription (a health worker's written instruction for a medicine), dosage (amount and timing), and substance abuse (using a substance in a harmful way or amount). They sort 6 short Kenyan scenario cards into 'correct use' or 'misuse' and explain each choice: e.g. (1) an adult follows the label of paracetamol 500 mg, taking 2 tablets every 6 hours; (2) a learner takes 10 paracetamol tablets in a day because a headache is severe; (3) a parent gives a child an adult dose; (4) a person takes antacid tablets all day after every meal for weeks; (5) a person buys medicine from a stall with no label or expiry date (linking to Lesson 8); (6) a person takes medicine prescribed by a clinic exactly as written. Learners also discuss the consumer's right to information on prescriptions, substance use and side effects (Citizenship).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use evidence, not opinion. Start with: We saw that F... so it can... G did not... so it...' After groups write, WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 groups to read their explanation and ask the others: 'What evidence in this explanation convinces you? What is missing?' Draw out the key idea: the antacid works because it reacts with and neutralises acid, paracetamol works on pain and fever by a different action, and both are harmful in excess. Give the four definitions only after learners have proposed their own; ask: 'Which word in our definition of substance abuse tells us a medicine can be misused?' (answer: harmful way or amount). For the scenario cards, cold-call 6 different learners, one per card: 'Is this use or misuse? Which evidence from today tells you?' Be sensitive: 'We talk about situations, not about anyone in this room. If you are worried about yourself or someone you know, see the guidance and counselling teacher.' Briefly stress that the Pharmacy and Poisons Board regulates medicines and that a prescription exists because a health worker chooses the medicine and dose for the person.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with scenario sorting. Learners make a claim (misuse or correct use), support it with evidence (label dose, 4 g maximum, effects), and give reasoning (properties and actions of the substance). Applying the same reasoning to new cases transfers the idea from the tray to everyday Kenyan life and shows that the properties-and-dose idea is general.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) explanations that include both parts: F reacts with acid and neutralises it; G acts on pain and fever and does not neutralise acid; (2) correct use of the terms drug, prescription, dosage and substance abuse; (3) at least 5 of 6 scenarios correctly classified with a reason that cites the label, dose or effects; (4) learners link to Lesson 8 by pointing to the missing label or expiry date in scenario 5; (5) respectful turn-taking and building on others' ideas. Ask 2 groups to restate a classmate's idea before adding their own.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board. Each group reads the questions from earlier lessons and decides which can now be answered fully or partly using Lesson 9 evidence (for example Wanjiru's question about why antacid and paracetamol differ, and the question on why too much is dangerous). They move answered questions to the 'Can answer now' column, write the evidence on a sticky note (such as 'F fizzes with acid, G does not' or '8 x 500 mg = 4 g maximum in 24 hours'), and add at least one new question, such as 'How do chemists test that a medicine is safe?' or 'Why do some medicines need a prescription?'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions can we answer better today? Place your sticky note with the evidence next to the question.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before groups move notes. Cold-call 3 groups: 'Which question did you answer, and what is your evidence?' Ask: 'What new question has today raised?' and add 2 to 3 new questions to the board. Link back to the KICD inquiry questions: 'How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? Today we only started: we saw why dosage matters. We will keep this question on the board.' Do not answer every question; mark open ones with a star for Lesson 10.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a tracking tool. Matching evidence to questions makes growth in understanding visible and shows learners that science is a continuing process: some questions are answered, others lead to new ones. It keeps the whole class connected to the anchoring phenomenon and the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that: (1) each group moves at least 1 question with a sticky note naming specific evidence from today; (2) evidence is accurate (the numbers 500 mg, 4 g, and F fizzes with acid); (3) each group adds at least 1 relevant new question; (4) learners can say what still needs to be answered. Tally the questions answered versus open on the board.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (model revision, 8 minutes): Using class model v2 (built in Lesson 6) as the starting point, each group adds a section on safe use: properties of a substance decide what it does; the dose decides whether it helps or harms; labels, prescriptions and correct dosage keep people safe. They draw an arrow from the properties of F and G on the tray to 'how the medicine works' to 'safe dose' to 'harm if misused'. Part B (poster project, remaining time and continued as homework): In groups of four, learners plan a poster to sensitise peers and the community on the risks of drug and substance use. Each poster must include: a clear title, 3 facts (one must be the paracetamol maximum of 4 g, i.e. 8 tablets of 500 mg, in 24 hours), an effect of antacid overuse, a message about following the label, prescription and health worker's advice, and where to get help (a health worker or the guidance and counselling teacher). Each member takes a role (ideas, drawing, wording, presenting), and the group agrees on the design by listening to every idea (Respect). Posters are displayed in the school corridor and shared with the community in Kisumu.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now answer: how do we use medicines safely? Add what we learned today to model v2. Show how the property of a medicine leads to its use and how the dose leads to safety.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 groups to explain one new arrow in their model. For the poster: 'Your poster must teach someone who was not in this lesson. Use one correct fact from our evidence. No scary pictures of people, and no names of real people.' Circulate and ask: 'How does your poster help a parent in Kisumu avoid giving a child an adult dose?' and 'Who made a decision in your group? Whose idea did you use?' Give the assessment criteria: accuracy, clarity, message, teamwork. Keep drafts for Lesson 10, when posters will be combined with the final model. Remind learners that all the lab rules (no tasting, goggles on) remain in force.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision and Communicating Information (NGSS SEP). Adding safety ideas to the model shows that the properties of matter, the action of a drug and the dosage are linked parts of one explanation. Designing a poster requires learners to select accurate evidence and communicate it to a real audience, which deepens understanding and builds the Communication and Collaboration and Citizenship competencies.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the revised model has at least 2 new connections, including property to action and dose to safety; (2) every poster has the paracetamol maximum (8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours), an antacid overuse effect and a safety message; (3) all 4 members have a role and have contributed; (4) learners explain their choices using evidence; (5) teacher uses a simple 3-point checklist (accurate, clear, teamwork) per group. Collect a one-sentence exit ticket: 'One thing I will do to use medicines safely is...'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners connect the property of reacting with acid (Lesson 2) to the antacid's action, rather than simply memorising it? (2) How many groups correctly worked out 8 x 500 mg = 4 g and used it in their poster? (3) Did any learners still believe 'more medicine means faster relief'? What evidence changed their minds? (4) Was every learner's voice heard in the groups (Respect)? (5) Was the discussion of substance abuse handled sensitively, and does any learner need follow-up with the guidance and counselling teacher? (6) Which new DQB questions should be given priority in Lesson 10? Plan to display posters and check them for accuracy before sharing with the community.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that antacid F fizzes in dilute vinegar (acid) while paracetamol G does not; both are tablets that behave differently (F crumbles into a cloudy suspension in water, G stays mostly intact). We read from the label that the adult paracetamol maximum is 8 tablets of 500 mg in 24 hours, and that antacid taken too often can cause constipation or diarrhoea.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a drug is a substance that changes how the body works, a prescription is a health worker's written instruction for a medicine, dosage is the amount and timing, and substance abuse is using a substance in a harmful way or amount. 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g is the paracetamol maximum in 24 hours; more can damage the liver. Children must not be given adult doses.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The antacid relieves heartburn because it reacts with and neutralises excess stomach acid, while paracetamol relieves pain and fever by a different action and does not neutralise acid. Both are harmful in excess, so we follow the label, prescription and a health worker's advice, and we share this message in posters to keep our school and community safe.
