LESSONS.title: Safe and Healthy Learning Environment and the Final Model: How Properties of Substances Shape the Products and Medicines We Use
LESSONS.aresKeywords: rights, responsibilities, safe and healthy learning environment, lab safety, Driving Question Board, final model, Final Explanation, properties, labels, dosage, substance abuse

slo.purpose: Learners finalise the class model and write a Final Explanation answering the driving question, and brainstorm their rights and responsibilities for a safe and healthy learning environment.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (a) explain that substances A-H behave differently because each has its own properties (solubility, magnetism, density, melting and burning behaviour, reaction with acid) which come from what it is made of; (b) state how chemists use such properties to choose, separate and make materials, including medicines; (c) state the rights and responsibilities of learners for a safe and healthy school and laboratory environment; (d) explain how labels, correct dosage and avoiding substance misuse keep people safe.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (comparing model v1 with the final model); constructing explanations (writing a Final Explanation using claim, evidence and reasoning); engaging in argument from evidence; obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (poster gallery); Communication and Collaboration; Citizenship (critical and constructive dialogue on rights and responsibilities).
slo.attitudes: Respect: learners show acceptance while appreciating the opinion of each member of the group. Learners advocate for a safe and healthy learning environment and take responsibility for their own and others' safety.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How are medicines for chronic diseases developed? 2. Do all substances around the world have the same properties and uses? 3. Why are food products, detergents and the things in the surrounding especially those that are man-made the way they are?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 10 closes the storyline. Learners use the evidence from Lessons 1-9 (the Kisumu tray A-H, the DQB, model v2 and the Lesson 9 posters) to finalise the model and answer the driving question. Learners also link the lab safety rules they have followed all along (goggles on, no tasting, heating by the teacher or supervised) to their rights and responsibilities for a safe and healthy school environment (PCI: life skills, safety and security).
slo.safetyNotes: No new practical heating is done in this lesson. Evidence is revisited from recorded results and labelled samples only. Reinforce lab rules: goggles on whenever chemicals or heat are present, no tasting or smelling directly, no heating without the teacher or a supervisor, wash hands after handling substances. Medicine packs used as props must be empty and clean. Do not let learners handle real tablets for tasting, and remind them that adult doses are not for children. Remind learners that Lesson 9 stated the maximum paracetamol dose is 8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours and that more can damage the liver.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the Kisumu school lab tray with eight substances (A table salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar). In this final lesson they first predict what a safe and healthy school needs and what the class model will look like, then gather evidence by reviewing the results recorded in Lessons 1-9 (the water test, heat test and the mixture M separation: 2.9 g iron, 2.8 g sand, 2.7 g salt, total 8.4 g recovered out of 9 g, loss 0.6 g). They brainstorm and present their rights and responsibilities for a safe and healthy learning environment and tie these to the safety rules used with the tray. Learners then complete the Driving Question Board by sorting questions into answered and partly answered, and compare model v1 (Lesson 3) with model v2 (Lesson 6) to build the final model. The lesson ends with each learner writing a Final Explanation that answers the driving question: How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in their Lesson 1 groups of four (Group 1: Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir; 8 groups, each with a tray). The teacher shows the tray A-H and the original DQB. In their notebooks, individually for 3 minutes, learners answer two prompts: (1) 'Without looking at your notes, what is the one idea that best explains why A-H behave so differently in water and heat?' (2) 'In our school and laboratory, what do I have a right to, and what must I take responsibility for so that everyone stays safe and healthy?' They then draw a quick sketch or list of what they think the final model should show (substances, properties, uses, safety). They share predictions in their group and note where they disagree.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the tray and say: 'This is the tray Mrs Achieng set up in Kisumu on day one. Today we finish our story. Before you open any notes, write what you think now.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. WAIT TIME: after asking 'What one idea explains why A-H behave so differently?', wait 10-15 seconds in silence before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups (not volunteers) to read their prediction aloud; record keywords on the board without correcting. Ask: 'Wanjiru asked early on why the antacid relieves heartburn but paracetamol relieves pain. What do you predict is the answer now?' Cold-call 2 more learners. Say: 'Your predictions are your starting point; we will check them against the evidence we have collected.' Circulate and look for learners who mention properties, dosage or labels.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit prior knowledge through individual prediction followed by Think-Pair-Share. Writing before talking makes each learner commit to an idea, so that when the evidence is reviewed they can see how their thinking has changed. Recording predictions on the board gives the class a visible 'before' picture to compare with the Final Explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 3 of 4 learners per group write a prediction that mentions properties or what substances are made of; (2) learners name at least one right (e.g. clean water, safe equipment, information on medicine) and one responsibility (e.g. following lab rules, not misusing substances); (3) learners link the antacid and paracetamol difference to different actions. Note learners who say 'they are just different' without reason, and revisit this in the Explain phase. Tick a class checklist for each group's participation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather evidence in two parts. Part A (about 12 minutes, evidence review): each group receives a recorded results card, a copy of their Lesson 2 and 3 data on the WATER TEST, HEAT TEST and mixture M separation, and the Lesson 9 posters on the wall. Using a table with columns for A-H, learners record at least one property for each substance: A salt dissolves completely, clear colourless solution, crackles on heating, no melting; B water; C sand sinks, does not dissolve, no change on heating; D sulphur floats, not wetted, melts at about 115 C then burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell; E iron filings sink, pulled out by a magnet, glow orange-red and turn dull blackish; F antacid crumbles into a cloudy white suspension and fizzes in dilute vinegar or lemon juice; G paracetamol stays mostly intact, crumbles slowly, no fizz, melts at about 169 C and browns; H sugar dissolves, melts at about 186 C, browns and chars with a caramel smell. They re-check mixture M: 3 g iron filings + 3 g sand + 3 g salt (9 g); magnet removes iron (2.9 g), filtration removes sand (2.8 g), evaporation recovers salt (2.7 g); total 8.4 g, loss 0.6 g from spillage and sticking to equipment. Part B (about 15 minutes, safe and healthy environment): groups brainstorm on sugar-paper their rights and responsibilities for a safe and healthy learning environment, using the lab safety rules practised with the tray (goggles on, no tasting, heating by the teacher or supervised) and the Lesson 8 and 9 ideas on labels, the maximum paracetamol dose of 8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours and the risks of misusing substances. Each group then does a 2-minute gallery presentation, and listeners give one 'star' (strength) and one 'wish' (suggestion) using respectful language.
framework.teacherMoves: Part A: Say: 'You are scientists reviewing your own data. Find the evidence, do not rely on memory.' Walk around with a checklist and ask each group: 'Which property lets you separate the iron from mixture M? Which property tells you the salt is still in the water?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after each question before prompting. Cold-call 3 groups to report the recovered masses and the loss calculation, 9 - 8.4 = 0.6 g, and ask 'Why is the total recovered less than 9 g?' Part B: Say: 'Our school is a place where everybody has the right to learn safely. With every right comes a responsibility. Write both.' Prompt with 'Which lab rule protected you when sulphur burned?' and 'Which responsibility protects a younger child from an adult paracetamol dose?' Remind learners of Respect: 'Listen fully before you respond; credit the idea of another member.' During gallery presentations cold-call 4 listeners to give a star and a wish. Clarify any misconception, for example that a medicine is safe because it is sold in a shop; correct with label, expiry date and dose information. Reinforce: no tasting and goggles on at all times.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence table (data review) plus Gallery Walk with Stars and Wishes. The table makes learners return to the recorded observations as the source of their claims, not memory. The gallery walk allows learners to compare their ideas on rights and responsibilities with those of other groups and to practise critical and constructive dialogue (Citizenship).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) completed tables with a correct property for all 8 substances and correct names A-H (e.g. calls A 'table salt', H 'sugar'); (2) correct use of 'dissolves' for A and H and 'does not dissolve' for C, D, E; (3) correct arithmetic 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g and 9 - 8.4 = 0.6 g; (4) each group lists at least 3 rights and 3 responsibilities, and links at least one to a lab rule; (5) stars and wishes are specific and respectful (observable respect indicator: members wait for each other and acknowledge ideas). Record on a rubric: meets, approaching, not yet.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write and discuss a Final Explanation answering the driving question. Step 1 (5 minutes): in groups, learners build a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) chart. Claim: substances behave differently because each has its own set of properties that come from what it is made of. Evidence: at least four pieces from the tray (e.g. A and H dissolve and cannot be filtered out; C and E do not dissolve and can be filtered or pulled out by a magnet; D burns with a blue flame while C does not; F fizzes in acid while G does not). Reasoning: chemists use properties to choose, separate and make materials, so mixture M was separated by magnetic separation, filtration and evaporation. Step 2 (5 minutes): learners explain the medicine puzzle, Wanjiru's question: the antacid (F, calcium carbonate with magnesium hydroxide) reacts with and neutralises excess stomach acid, relieving heartburn; paracetamol (G, 500 mg) relieves pain and fever by a different action and does not neutralise acid; both are harmful in excess (paracetamol over 4 g in 24 hours can damage the liver; too much antacid can cause constipation or diarrhoea). Step 3 (10 minutes): each learner individually writes a Final Explanation of 8-10 sentences answering how properties help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how we use them safely, and links it to the three KICD key inquiry questions (medicines for chronic diseases, different properties and uses of substances, why food products and detergents are the way they are). Examples to include: Kericho tea, Magadi soda ash, Mumias or Nzoia sugar, Kenyan pharmaceutical manufacturers in Nairobi, KEBS Diamond Mark, Pharmacy and Poisons Board, and ugali or nyama choma as everyday food chemistry.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A good scientist does not only say what happened, but why. Use Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.' Model one sentence on the board: 'I claim that sand and salt behave differently because ...' and ask learners to finish it. WAIT TIME: after 'Why does the antacid fizz in vinegar but paracetamol does not?' wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'Which property did chemists use to separate iron from sand and salt? Which property did we use for salt?' Cold-call 2 more learners. Probe: 'If a friend says, I took six paracetamol tablets at once because my head hurts a lot, what would you tell them?' Cold-call 2 learners to respond using the label (1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets in 24 hours) and say that children must not be given adult doses. Press for evidence: 'What data show that? Point to your table.' Circulate during individual writing, and use sentence starters ('because', 'which shows that', 'therefore') for learners who need support. Do not re-teach earlier lessons; refer learners to the branches (Lesson 5), industries (Lesson 6), labels (Lesson 8) and drug and dosage ideas (Lesson 9) as they have been taught.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a Final Explanation. CER requires learners to connect a general claim about properties to specific evidence from the tray and to the reasoning that links the two, so that the explanation answers the driving question rather than just listing facts. Applying it to the antacid and paracetamol puzzle transfers understanding to a new, real-life situation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the claim states that properties come from what a substance is made of; (2) at least 3 correct pieces of tray evidence with correct units (g, mL, C, mg); (3) the reasoning links properties to a use (separation of mixture M, choosing medicines, making food and household products); (4) the antacid is explained as neutralising acid and paracetamol as acting on pain and fever, not acid; (5) the explanation includes safe use: reading labels, correct dosage (maximum 4 g of paracetamol in 24 hours), no adult doses for children, avoiding substance misuse. Score with a 4-point rubric (claim, evidence, reasoning, safety). Collect Final Explanations to identify learners who need follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners complete the Driving Question Board. The class DQB from Lesson 1 (with questions added across lessons) is displayed. Step 1: each group receives 4-5 sticky notes with questions from the DQB and sorts them into three columns: 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New question'. For each answered question, learners write the lesson number and the evidence that answered it (e.g. 'Why can some mixtures be separated easily while others cannot?' answered by mixture M: magnet, filtration, evaporation; 'Why does the antacid relieve heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain?' answered by acid-neutralising action versus action on pain and fever). Step 2: learners post one new question that they still wonder about (e.g. how Kenyan pharmaceutical manufacturers in Nairobi test medicines before sale, or how the Pharmacy and Poisons Board checks them). Step 3: the class agrees on a final sentence that answers the driving question and writes it at the top of the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board is our record of learning. Let us see how far we have come.' Give each group their notes and say: 'Decide where each question belongs and prove it with evidence from a lesson.' WAIT TIME: after asking 'Which questions are still partly answered?' wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups (one question each) to justify their sorting and ask 'What evidence supports that?' Ask: 'Which of the three KICD key inquiry questions did we answer best? Which one needs more study?' Cold-call 2 learners. Probe respectfully when learners disagree: 'Amina and Kipchirchir see this differently. Each of you, say the other's idea in your own words first.' Record the agreed class answer. Point out that the unanswered questions will be taken up in later strands, such as 1.2 The Atom (How are electrons arranged in an atom?), without teaching that content now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Sorting questions on the Driving Question Board (answered, partly answered, new) with evidence justification. This turns the DQB from a list of curiosity into a record of learning, and makes learners trace each answer back to specific evidence and lessons, showing the progress of understanding over time.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) each sorted question has a correct lesson number and a piece of evidence; (2) learners can distinguish a fully answered question from a partly answered one, with a reason; (3) at least one new, testable question is posted by each group; (4) learners paraphrase peers' ideas before disagreeing (observable Respect). Tally on a checklist how many groups placed 'Why do powders behave differently?' and 'How does the antacid work?' as answered with evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners finalise the class model. Step 1 (5 minutes): each group displays model v1 (Lesson 3: classifying substances as elements, compounds or mixtures and the first ideas on properties) and model v2 (Lesson 6: revised with the uses in Kenyan industries). Learners list what has changed. Step 2 (10 minutes): groups redraw a final model on a large sheet with 4 parts: (a) what the substances are made of, classified as elements (D sulphur, E iron), compounds (A salt, B water, H sugar, calcium carbonate in F) and mixtures (mixture M; tablets are mixtures of an active ingredient with binders); (b) their properties (solubility, magnetism, density, melting and burning behaviour, reaction with acid); (c) how chemists use the properties (separate by magnet, filtration and evaporation; choose and make medicines, foods such as sugar from Mumias or Nzoia, tea from Kericho, soda ash from Magadi, and other products); (d) how we stay safe (labels with the KEBS Diamond Mark, expiry date, ingredients, caution messages; correct dosage, e.g. paracetamol maximum 8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours; avoiding substance abuse; lab safety rules and learner rights and responsibilities). Step 3 (5 minutes): a spokesperson from each group explains how the final model differs from v1 in a model comparison, completing the sentence 'At first we thought ..., now we know ... because ...'. The class agrees on one final model and displays it beside the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A model is a tool for explaining. Compare v1 and v2 with what you now know, and improve it.' Provide sentence frames for the comparison: 'In v1 we showed ..., in the final model we added ... because the evidence shows ...'. Ask: 'What was missing from model v1 that we needed to explain why the antacid and paracetamol differ?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after this question. Cold-call 4 spokespersons to compare v1 with the final model. Ask: 'Where on your model do safety and labels fit? Why must safety be part of a chemistry model?' Cold-call 2 learners. Check that substances are called by letters A-H and correct names, that only 'filtration', 'magnetic separation' and 'evaporation' are used, and that classification matches the conventions. After the class agrees on the final model, ask each learner to complete the summary table individually and make a personal commitment to one safety responsibility. Close with: 'Chemistry helps us to understand how drugs interact with the body and to recognise the risks of drug abuse. You now have the tools to use that knowledge safely, at school, at home and in your community.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision and comparison (v1, v2 to final). Placing the models side by side lets learners see how their understanding grew from sorting and classifying to explaining properties, uses and safety. The sentence frame 'At first we thought..., now we know... because...' forces explicit reasoning about change in ideas, linking the evidence collected to the final explanation of the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the final model includes all four parts (what substances are made of, properties, uses, safety) with correct classification of A-H; (2) at least two changes from v1 are named and justified with evidence; (3) the model includes the antacid neutralising acid versus paracetamol acting on pain and fever; (4) safety (labels, dosage, rights and responsibilities) is represented, not only chemistry content; (5) spokespersons use scientific vocabulary correctly. Use a 3-level rubric (complete, partial, incomplete) and record who needs support. Final check: learners' summary tables are consistent with their Final Explanation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on: (1) Did learners use properties, not just description, to explain why A-H behave differently? Which groups still say 'they are just different'? (2) Could learners explain why the antacid (F) and paracetamol (G) work differently, and state the maximum paracetamol dose of 4 g in 24 hours with the reason? (3) Did the brainstorm on rights and responsibilities lead to real commitments (for example following lab rules, reading labels, not sharing medicines, not misusing substances), and did learners show Respect when others spoke? (4) Which learners struggled with the claim-evidence-reasoning structure and what support (sentence starters, worked example) helped? (5) How did the final model differ from v1, and did every group include safety? (6) Which DQB questions remained 'partly answered' and how will they be followed up in Sub-Strand 1.2 The Atom? (7) Was wait time of 10-15 seconds used consistently, and did cold-calling give quieter learners, including girls, a voice? Note changes to make next time.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: You have worked with the Kisumu tray of eight substances (A table salt, B water, C sand, D sulphur, E iron filings, F antacid tablet, G paracetamol tablet, H sugar) over ten lessons. Use your own tray evidence and your learning from the lessons to answer the Driving Question: How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely? Answer each section in the space under its prompt. Use the letters A-H and the exact names of the substances. Use numbers and units (g, mL, C, mg) from your own results where you can. Write in full sentences and show your working for any calculation. Remember our class value of respect: write in your own words and be ready to listen to other groups' ideas.

sections.title: Section 1: Same look, different behaviour
sections.prompt:
Look at the data table from the Kisumu tray tests (1 level spatula, about 2 g, of each solid in 50 mL of water at about 25 C; heat test done by the teacher).

| Substance | In water | Heat test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A table salt | dissolves, clear solution | crackles, no melting |
| C sand | sinks, stays visible | no change |
| D sulphur | floats, not wetted | melts at about 115 C, then burns with blue flame |
| E iron filings | sink, pulled out by a magnet | glow orange-red, turn dull blackish |
| H sugar | dissolves, clear solution | melts at about 186 C, browns, then chars |

(a) Wanjiru noticed that several of these substances look like powders. Why do substances that look alike behave so differently? Use evidence from at least three substances in the table. (b) Name two physical properties and one chemical property that you used to tell the substances apart.
sections.exemplar: (a) Looking at a substance does not tell us how it will behave. Each substance has its own set of properties, and these come from what it is made of. A salt and H sugar both dissolve in water and give clear solutions, but C sand does not dissolve and sinks, and D sulphur floats and is not wetted. E iron filings also do not dissolve, but a magnet pulls them out. In the heat test, H sugar melts at about 186 C and chars, D sulphur melts at about 115 C and burns, but C sand does not change. So powders that look alike have different properties. (b) Physical properties: solubility (salt and sugar dissolve, sand does not) and magnetism (iron is pulled by a magnet); melting point is also acceptable. Chemical property: burning (sulphur burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell, but sand does not burn); reacting with acid is also acceptable.

sections.title: Section 2: Separating mixture M
sections.prompt:
Mixture M was 3 g iron filings + 3 g sand + 3 g salt, a total of 9 g, in water. Group 1 separated it in three steps and recorded the masses recovered: iron 2.9 g, sand 2.8 g (after drying), salt 2.7 g.

(a) Name the method that removed each of the three substances and explain why that method worked for that substance. (b) Why could the salt not be removed by filtration or a magnet? (c) Calculate the total mass recovered and the mass lost. Give one reason for the loss.
sections.exemplar: (a) Iron was removed by magnetic separation, because iron is pulled by a magnet and sand and salt are not. Sand was removed by filtration, because sand does not dissolve, so its grains are trapped on the filter paper while the salt solution passes through. Salt was recovered by evaporation of the filtrate, which leaves the salt behind when the water goes away. (b) Salt dissolves in water, so it is mixed in the water and passes through the filter paper. It is not magnetic, so a magnet cannot pull it out. Only evaporation separates it. (c) Total recovered = 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g. Loss = 9 - 8.4 = 0.6 g. The loss was caused by spillage and by some material sticking to the equipment.

sections.title: Section 3: Classifying and the meaning of Chemistry
sections.prompt: (a) Write the meaning of Chemistry and of matter. (b) Classify D sulphur, A table salt and mixture M as an element, a compound or a mixture, and give a reason for each. (c) Name the five branches of chemistry and say which branch you would link to the separation of mixture M.
sections.exemplar: (a) Chemistry is the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. (b) D sulphur is an element, like E iron. A table salt is a compound because it is a substance made of more than one kind of element joined together (sodium chloride), like B water and H sugar. Mixture M is a mixture because it contains iron filings, sand and salt that are not joined together and could be separated by magnet, filtration and evaporation. (c) The five branches are organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biochemistry. The separation of mixture M links to analytical chemistry.

sections.title: Section 4: Medicines and using them safely
sections.prompt: Wanjiru asked why the antacid and paracetamol work differently. (a) Using what you saw in the vinegar test, explain how F antacid tablet relieves heartburn and how G paracetamol tablet is different. (b) The adult paracetamol label says 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours. Calculate the maximum number of milligrams and grams allowed in 24 hours if the maximum is 8 tablets, and say what can happen if more is taken. (c) Otieno's customer wanted to give an adult dose to a small child. What advice would you give, and which items on a label help a buyer to be safe?
sections.exemplar: (a) F antacid fizzes when dropped into dilute vinegar, which is an acid, so it reacts with and neutralises acid. Heartburn is caused by too much acid in the stomach, so the antacid relieves it by neutralising that acid. G paracetamol does not fizz in vinegar, so it does not neutralise acid. It relieves pain and fever by a different action. (b) 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g in 24 hours. Taking more than this can damage the liver. (c) Do not give a child an adult dose. Read the label, follow the correct dosage and ask a health worker or pharmacist for advice. Label items that help a buyer are the quality mark (such as the KEBS Diamond Mark), the expiry date, the ingredients and preservatives, nutritional information and caution messages. Too much antacid taken too often can also cause constipation or diarrhoea, so both medicines are harmful in excess. Avoiding substance abuse (using a substance in a harmful way or amount) keeps people safe.

sections.title: Section 5: Final Explanation
sections.prompt: Write a connected explanation of 8-10 sentences that answers the Driving Question: How do the different properties of substances around us help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how do we use them safely? Use evidence from the Kisumu tray, including at least one number from your results. Include (i) why substances that look alike behave differently, (ii) how chemists use properties to separate or make materials, with at least one Kenyan industry or example, (iii) why the antacid and paracetamol work differently and why both are harmful in excess, and (iv) one responsibility you will take for a safe and healthy environment at school and at home.
sections.exemplar: Each substance on the Kisumu tray has its own set of properties, such as solubility, magnetism, melting point and burning, and these come from what the substance is made of. That is why powders that look alike behave differently: A salt and H sugar dissolve and cannot be filtered out, but C sand and E iron filings do not dissolve, and D sulphur burns with a blue flame while sand does not. Chemists use these properties to choose, separate and make materials. For example, in mixture M we used a magnet to remove iron (2.9 g), filtration to remove sand (2.8 g) and evaporation to recover salt (2.7 g), which shows that the method must match the property. Kenyan industries do the same: Magadi soda ash and Mumias and Nzoia sugar depend on separating substances, and pharmaceutical manufacturers in Nairobi choose materials by their properties to make medicines. The antacid F neutralises excess stomach acid because it reacts with acid, so it relieves heartburn, while paracetamol G relieves pain and fever by a different action and does not neutralise acid. Both are harmful in excess: adults must not take more than 8 x 500 mg = 4 g of paracetamol in 24 hours because it can damage the liver, and too much antacid can cause constipation or diarrhoea. Labels with a quality mark, expiry date, ingredients and caution messages, correct dosage, a health worker's advice and avoiding substance abuse turn this knowledge into safe use. Children must never be given adult doses. At school I will take responsibility by wearing goggles, not tasting substances and following my teacher's safety rules, and at home I will read labels and keep medicines away from small children.

lessons.explained: Explain in one or two sentences, using evidence, why substances that look like powders behave differently and why salt and sugar cannot be filtered out while sand and iron can be separated by filtration or magnetic separation, and how this links to the driving question about medicines, foods and safety.

lessons.title: Matter Continued: Classifying Substances and Building Class Model v1
lessons.observed: We observed that A salt and H sugar dissolve completely, C sand and E iron filings do not dissolve, E is pulled out by a magnet, D sulphur floats and burns with a blue flame and sharp smell, and F antacid fizzes in vinegar while G paracetamol does not. lessons.explained: The substances behave differently because each has its own properties, which come from what it is made of. Iron and sand can be pulled out or filtered, while salt and sugar dissolve and cannot be filtered out. The antacid works because it neutralises acid, paracetamol works on pain and fever by a different action, and both are harmful in excess, so we follow labels and correct dosage.

lessons.title: Meaning of Chemistry as a Field of Science: Defining Chemistry from the Tray Evidence
lessons.observed: What did you observe about the tray substances A-H that shows Chemistry studies matter? For example: salt A and sugar H dissolve, sand C and iron E do not, sulphur D burns with a blue flame, and the antacid F fizzes in vinegar while paracetamol G does not.
lessons.learned: What did you learn about the meaning of Chemistry? Chemistry is the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
lessons.explained: How does the definition of Chemistry help explain why the antacid relieves heartburn while paracetamol relieves pain, and why chemists in Kenya need to know the properties of substances to make medicines, foods and detergents safely?

lessons.title: Branches of Chemistry: Matching the Five Branches to the Kisumu Tray
lessons.observed: We observed data from the Kisumu tray: sugar H and paracetamol G melt and brown at about 186 C and 169 C; salt A dissolves and iron E is pulled out by a magnet; sulphur D melts at about 115 C; mixture M (9 g) was separated by magnet (2.9 g), filtration (2.8 g) and evaporation (2.7 g); the antacid F fizzes in vinegar while paracetamol G does not.
lessons.learned: Chemistry has five branches: organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biochemistry. Each answers different questions about the same substances, and one substance can belong to more than one branch. Listening respectfully to every group member's opinion improved our answers.
lessons.explained: The tray puzzles are answered by different branches working together: organic (sugar H and paracetamol G), inorganic (salt A and iron E), physical (melting points), analytical (separating mixture M) and biochemistry (how the antacid F and paracetamol G act in the body). This helps chemists make and test medicines, foods and other products safely, which moves us toward answering the driving question.

lessons.title: Importance of Chemistry in Kenya: From the Kisumu Tray to Our Industries (Model v2)
lessons.observed: Record what you observed: the properties of A-H (salt and sugar dissolve; sand and iron do not; iron is pulled by a magnet; sulphur melts and burns with a blue flame and sharp choking smell; F fizzes in dilute vinegar but G does not), and the Kenyan industry examples you studied.
lessons.learned: Record what you learned: chemistry is important in agriculture, pharmaceutical, medicine, manufacturing, entertainment, nuclear, food, sports and energy industries because industries choose, separate and make materials using properties; the antacid neutralises acid, paracetamol relieves pain and fever, and the adult maximum is 8 x 500 mg = 4 g in 24 hours.
lessons.explained: Explain how this helps answer the driving question: use evidence from the tray and at least two industries to explain how properties help chemists make medicines, foods and other products, and how labels, correct dosage and avoiding substance misuse keep people safe. Describe what you added to model v2.

lessons.title: Careers in Chemistry: Who Works with the Kisumu Tray Substances, and Who Gets to Choose?
lessons.observed: We observed that careers such as pharmacist, analytical chemist, laboratory technician and quality control officer use the properties of substances we saw in the tray: F antacid reacts with acid, G paracetamol does not, and mixture M was separated by magnet, filtration and evaporation (2.9 g, 2.8 g and 2.7 g recovered out of 9 g).
lessons.learned: We learned that chemistry offers many careers in medicine, industry and testing, and that gender stereotypes are fixed ideas that can wrongly limit who chooses these careers.
lessons.explained: We can explain that people in chemistry careers use properties to make, separate and check products such as medicines, and that safety through labels and correct dosage matters, and that girls and boys can both choose these careers; this adds to our answer to the driving question.

lessons.title: Consumer Protection and Product Labels: Reading the Story a Label Tells
lessons.observed: We observed the labels on a paracetamol 500 mg box (G), an antacid pack (F), a maize flour packet, a juice carton and a detergent bottle. We found the KEBS Diamond Mark, expiry dates, ingredients and preservatives, nutritional information, and caution and dose messages, and we noticed where information was missing.
lessons.learned: We learned that labels protect consumers by giving information on quality, how long a product is safe to use, what it contains, and how to use it safely. The paracetamol label says adults take 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, with a maximum of 8 tablets (4000 mg = 4 g) in 24 hours, because more can damage the liver. Antacid taken too often can cause constipation or diarrhoea, and children must not be given adult doses.
lessons.explained: Substances like the antacid (F) and paracetamol (G) have different properties and uses, so their labels give different instructions. Labels turn what chemists know about the properties of substances into safe-use messages for the consumer. This helps answer the driving question about how we use products safely, and prepares us to study drugs, dosage and substance abuse in Lesson 9.

lessons.title: Drugs and Substance Abuse: Why the Dose Makes the Difference
lessons.observed: We observed that antacid F fizzes in dilute vinegar (acid) while paracetamol G does not; both are tablets that behave differently (F crumbles into a cloudy suspension in water, G stays mostly intact). We read from the label that the adult paracetamol maximum is 8 tablets of 500 mg in 24 hours, and that antacid taken too often can cause constipation or diarrhoea.
lessons.learned: We learned that a drug is a substance that changes how the body works, a prescription is a health worker's written instruction for a medicine, dosage is the amount and timing, and substance abuse is using a substance in a harmful way or amount. 8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g is the paracetamol maximum in 24 hours; more can damage the liver. Children must not be given adult doses.
lessons.explained: The antacid relieves heartburn because it reacts with and neutralises excess stomach acid, while paracetamol relieves pain and fever by a different action and does not neutralise acid. Both are harmful in excess, so we follow the label, prescription and a health worker's advice, and we share this message in posters to keep our school and community safe.
